events.text: One summer midnight you look down at yourself and you are not there. Where your beak was is the Willow, eight stars curved like a hook. Your neck is the Seven Stars, your crop the Extended Net, which is the kitchen of heaven and keeps its guests fed. The Wings are your wings. The Chariot is the wind under your tail. And in front of your head, like two lamps carried before a procession, the Well and the Ghost. The south of the sky is a bird, and the bird is you.

choices.text: Count your stars, one by one, beak to tail

effects.log: It takes a whole night. Willow, eight. Seven Stars, seven. Net, six. Wings, twenty-two, which you count twice because they keep moving. Chariot, four. At dawn you know your own body the way a farmer knows a field, stone by stone, and the farmers below look up at a sky that seems somehow tidier.

choices.text: Spread the Wings, just to see what it does

effects.log: The Wings open across a quarter of the sky. On earth, every traveller far from home on that road, that ferry, that pass, stops and looks south and feels, for no reason, that someone is waiting up. That is what the Wings are for. You fold them carefully.

choices.text: Sing the names of the seven, the way the south sings everything

effects.log: Well, Ghost, Willow, Stars, Net, Wings, Chariot. Your voice goes down through the summer night like heat off a roof tile. An astronomer on a tower in the capital writes "the southern mansions unusually bright, and possibly singing" and then crosses out the last part.

events.text: Now that you are stars, you can see your fires from above: every fire you ever gave and kept, burning on the dark land as a small red star of its own, and each one answering a feather in you. The houses round them are warm. But there are dark places too, gaps in your plumage like moth holes, and you know each one: a fire that went out, a fire you called home, a fire that ran.

choices.text: Fly down and relight the dark place where the Hearth was

effects.log: A widowed farmer in a cold house on the edge of the paddies, the stove dead a week. You drop a coal in it from very high, and it lands exactly. The gap in your crop closes with a feeling like a swallowed sob. (The Hearth burns again.)

choices.text: Relight the dark place where the Lantern was

effects.log: A ferry on a wide brown river, the landing lantern gone dark for years. You set a coal in it at dusk. That night a child lost on the far bank sees it and walks toward it until the ferry-keeper's hand closes on a small cold hand. (The Lantern burns again.)

choices.text: Relight the dark place where the Beacon was

effects.log: The beacon hill on the southern coast, its five chimneys cold, the post half abandoned. You light one chimney: all is well. A young soldier who was asleep at the post wakes, sees one fire burning that nobody lit, and decides to say nothing about it to anybody, ever, and to keep it. (The Beacon burns again.)

choices.text: Leave the gaps. Learn their shapes

effects.log: You do not fill them yet. You learn them instead, the way an old soldier learns his scars: this one the year you slept too long, this one the keeper who turned, this one the slope that burned. A bird of stars who forgets its dark places will make more.

events.text: Beside the Well, which governs the law and the waters, hangs one small fierce star the astronomers call the Axe. Its charge is excess: it watches whatever grows past its measure. Tonight, for the first time, it is not watching the Well. It has turned, very slowly, and it is watching you.

choices.text: Let it look. Hold still and let the Axe see all of it

effects.log: It sees the fires that ran, the tempers you let out, the swallowed things still smouldering under your breast feathers. It looks a long time. Then it turns back to the Well. Not a pardon. A note. You feel lighter for having been read.

choices.text: Sing your temper out before it can measure it

effects.log: You sing everything you swallowed in the last century at the Axe, verse after verse, until there is nothing left in you hot enough to be excess. The Axe listens with what you could swear is amusement and turns back to its Well.

choices.text: Cover it with a wing. Nobody measures the south

effects.log: You spread a Wing across the Axe and keep it there for a month of nights. It is very hard to hold a wing still for a month. All the while it watches you through your own feathers, and you burn quietly with something that is not quite shame. (-2 health)

events.text: The Chariot, the four stars under your tail, governs the wind, and this year it slips. A hot dry wind gets loose and goes down across the south for a whole month, out of the southwest, the kind of wind that finds every fire and makes it bigger. Every one of your fires leans the same way.

choices.text: Hold the Chariot steady with your tail

ok.log: You clamp your tail round the four stars and haul. For three days the sky creaks. Then the wind drops all at once, and on earth a whole province of farmers looks up from their scorched seedlings and says, the wind has stopped, as if winds stopped by themselves.

fail.log: The Chariot drags you half across the sky before you let go. The wind runs its month. A barn burns in a county you have never seen; nobody dies; it is still ash on your record. (Ash +1, -12 health)

choices.text: Ride the wind down to the Field Fire before it spreads

effects.log: You ride the hot wind to the burnt slope where your Field Fire lives, and rub it new with apricot and jujube, summer's wood, before the wind can get into it. The farmers bank the new fire low in the lee of a rock. The wind goes past it like a dog that has been told no.

choices.text: Fly the circuit and warn every keeper

effects.log: A month of flying from fire to fire against the wind: bank it low, wet the thatch, keep the children in. Not one of your fires runs. You land at the end of it so tired your feathers are grey at the tips. (-6 health)

events.text: The last red feather that was only a feather goes up one autumn night and does not come down. It hangs there, a new faint star at the tip of your tail. There is nothing left of you now that is not either a fire on earth or a star in the south. The astronomers argue about the new star for a year and then give it a name. It is the name of the youngest of a house, centuries dead, which nobody can explain.

choices.text: Shine on it, so the name keeps

effects.log: The star stays bright all winter. Children in the south are told to find it before bed. None of them knows whose name it is. It is enough that someone says it.

choices.text: Let it fade back to an ordinary star

effects.log: You let it go faint. A star with a name is a thing people make pilgrimages to, and set up shrines under, and quarrel about. The youngest of the house would have hated that. You keep the name for yourself.

events.text: At the heart of the Ghost, the mansion in front of your head that keeps the rites of the dead, there is a pale thing: not a star, a breath of light, like frost on a window. The old astronomers called it the Heaped Corpses, and were not joking. Tonight you see what it is for. Thin grey shapes are drifting up to it from the land below, from graves nobody sweeps, the way moths come to a lamp.
events.arc: The Pale Thing in the Ghost

choices.text: Watch them, and learn who they are

effects.log: A soldier from a war nobody remembers. A child of a family that died out. A clerk whose sons became monks. The dead whose rites have stopped, all of them, come here to wait, because nobody below lights a candle for them any more, and the pale thing is the last candle there is.

choices.text: Flare red at them, the yang colour

effects.log: The grey shapes scatter off your red like mist off a hot roof and drift back again when you dim. They are not afraid of you. They are only cold. You feel, for the first time in centuries, a little foolish.

choices.text: Ask the pale thing what it wants

effects.log: "Nothing," says the pale thing, in a voice like a whisper through rice paper. "I keep the ones nobody keeps. I am very tired. You are a rite candle, little bird. Did you know?"

events.text: The grey shapes rising to the Ghost come thicker this year, a whole drift of them from one county in the south. You know that county. A Rite Candle of yours should be burning there, on the altar shelf of a lineage hall, and its dead should be at rest. No candle burns, and the eldest of the lineage is dead without anyone to take the rite on.
events.arc: The Pale Thing in the Ghost

choices.text: Go down, relight the candle, and find the lineage a new eldest

effects.log: The lineage hall is dusty and the tablets are crooked. You set a coal on the altar and the candle takes, and a great-grandchild who came only to sell the hall sees it from the yard, and does not sell it. The grey drift going up from that county thins, and stops. (The Rite Candle burns again.)

choices.text: Sing the drifting dead their own names, on the way up

effects.log: You do not know their names, so you ask, and each one tells you, faintly, and you sing it back louder. It is not a rite. It is the next best thing. Some of them stop at your song and go down again, back to their graves, to wait for somebody to remember.

choices.text: Fly down and shout at the descendants

effects.log: You come down on the lineage hall roof at noon, burning, and tell the great-grandsons exactly what you think of them. The roof ridge catches. They put it out. They light the candles that night, every one, out of terror, which is a kind of rite. (Ash +1)

events.text: Among the grey shapes drifting up to the Ghost, one turns its face toward you, and you know it. A round face, a padded jacket, cupped hands. The youngest of the house you were born in, who first knelt and blew on you, centuries ago. The house has kept the fire. Nobody has kept the rite for the one who kept it first.
events.arc: The Pale Thing in the Ghost

choices.text: Sing the name, the whole night, until the shape turns back

effects.log: You sing the one name you never forgot. The shape stops rising. It listens. Near dawn it turns and goes down, slowly, toward a village you know, and that winter a child in that house asks for the first time who used to keep the fire jar, and an old aunt tells her.

choices.text: Let it go up. It has earned a quiet place

effects.log: You let it rise into the pale thing and be kept. It is not cold there. You check, after, and it is not. You go and sit on the fire jar of that house for a whole winter anyway, burning very gently.

choices.text: Make it a star in your own feathers

effects.log: You take it into the Net, the crop of heaven, the kitchen that keeps the guests fed, and it becomes a faint warm star there. Nobody on earth notices. You notice every night.

events.text: The pale thing in the Ghost has grown. It has kept so many forgotten dead for so long that it has begun to pull at the living: in three counties people dream of grey rooms and wake tired, and the old die a little earlier than they should. It does not mean harm. It is only very full.
events.arc: The Pale Thing in the Ghost

choices.text: Burn red through it, once, and send the dead on

ok.log: You fly through the pale thing at full heat, the yang colour from beak to tail. The dead in it do not burn. They warm, and the warm ones go on, wherever the dead go when someone remembers them once more. The pale thing shrinks to a breath of frost again. It thanks you, faintly.

fail.log: You go in too hot and too fast. The dead scatter across three provinces as grey nightmares for a year. They settle again. It is still your doing. (Ash +1, -14 health)

choices.text: Light candles for them below, county by county

effects.log: It takes twenty years. You perch on altar shelves in lineage halls and village shrines and abandoned temples, and wherever a candle should burn you see that one does. The pale thing empties slowly, the right way, a little each spring. (-8 health)

choices.text: Leave it. The Ghost keeps the dead; you keep fires

effects.log: You leave it. The dreams go on in three counties. In time someone else, a monk, a shaman with a bell, begins to light candles there. It takes them a century. You could have done it in twenty years. You know it.

events.text: Noon on the summer solstice, the longest day, and you go up. Not to the sun: through it. It is white inside, and loud, a roar like a kiln with every door open, and at the centre of it, black as a cooking pot, stands a crow. It has three legs. It looks at you with an expression you know very well, from the kitchen god of your first stove. It is the expression of someone whose fire you have just walked into.

choices.text: Bow, first and low, as the south does

effects.log: You bow inside the sun, which singes even you. The crow looks at you a long while. Then it bows back, all three legs bending, and says, "Well. At least somebody was raised properly." You come out the far side of noon red to the bone.

choices.text: Keep flying. You were only passing through

effects.log: You go straight through and out the far side of noon. Behind you the crow caws once, a sound like a pot lid slammed. Every rooster in the south crows at midday and nobody below knows why.

choices.text: Ask it what it is doing in there

effects.log: "Carrying it," says the crow, as if it were obvious. "Every day. East to west. Somebody has to." It looks at your tail. "You are the one who keeps setting fire to the south. I have been meaning to speak to you."

events.text: The three-legged crow has sent word, by a hot wind, that noon is its. Not the south's, not summer's: its own. It has carried the sun through noon since before there were birds, and a red upstart who crosses it on the solstice and makes every rooster in the south crow at the wrong hour is a breach of manners. It wants you to stop.

choices.text: Go and argue it out inside the sun, properly, all day

ok.log: You argue from dawn to dusk. Summer, you say, is noon spread over a season. Noon, says the crow, is summer folded into an hour. Somewhere in the late afternoon you both notice you are agreeing. It is extremely annoying for both of you.

fail.log: It talks you down. It has been talking to the sun for longer than you have been fire, and you come out of noon with nothing to say and something hot stuck in your throat. (-10 health)

choices.text: Fight it for the solstice

ok.log: Beak to beak in the white heart of noon. It is very old and very strong and it has three legs to your two, and you still knock it a wingspan off the middle of the sun. It stands up, shakes itself, and laughs a black laugh. "There you are," it says. "I wondered."

fail.log: It puts you out of the sun with one kick of the third leg. You fall a long way through a bleached sky and land in a millpond in the southern hills, which boils. (-22 health)

choices.text: Stay off noon for a year, out of courtesy, and see what it does

effects.log: You give it the solstice. The day is short a little warmth, and the barley a little slow, and the crow, at the end of the year, sends you one black feather on the hot wind. You do not know what it means. You keep it.

events.text: The sun rises late and dim one spring morning, and later and dimmer the next. A message comes on a pale, embarrassed wind: the three-legged crow has a bad leg. The third one. It can carry the sun, it says, but slowly, and noon will be thin for a month, and the seedlings will notice. It does not ask. It would rather fall out of the sky.

choices.text: Carry the sun through noon for it, for the month

ok.log: A month under the sun, your back to it, wings braced, the heat of it going through you like water through a sieve. The seedlings never notice. On the last day the crow limps up beside you and takes the weight, and says, gruffly, "You hold it crooked." That is thanks, from a crow.

fail.log: You hold it for nineteen days and then it slides, and you go down under it into the southern sea, which hisses for a week. The crow carries the last eleven days itself, on two legs. Neither of you mentions it again. (-35 health)
fail.deathCause: burned out under the noon sun, carrying it for a lame crow

choices.text: Fly ahead of the sun at dawn and warm the seedlings yourself

effects.log: Every dawn for a month you go low across the paddies before the thin sun is up, breathing on the seedlings. They grow. The crow, when it is better, says only, "I saw." (-8 health)

choices.text: Leave noon thin. The crow would not thank you

effects.log: A thin month. The seedlings are a little late, the barley a little short. The crow mends. Some debts are better never run up between two proud birds.

events.text: On a slow afternoon at the edge of the sun the crow tells you about the tombs. In the old kingdom of the north they painted it on the ceilings of the dead, it says: inside a wheel of fire, three-legged, crested, high over everything. "And you," it says, "they painted on the south wall. Below. By the door." It lets that sit.

choices.text: Say the door is where the guard stands

effects.log: "Hm," says the crow. It thinks about it for a whole day, which for a crow inside the sun is a long time. "Hm," it says again, in a different tone, and the next time it speaks of the tombs it says "we".

choices.text: Ask it what the dead looked at, the ceiling or the door

effects.log: "The door," says the crow at last, unwillingly. "Everyone looks at the door. That is where they hope someone will come in." It is quiet the rest of the afternoon. So are you.

choices.text: Laugh until noon wobbles

effects.log: You laugh so hard that noon itself shakes, and on earth a whole province sees the sun shiver at midday and runs for the shaman. The crow is livid, and then, much later, not. (Ash +1)

events.text: Noon on the solstice again, and the crow is waiting for you in the white heart of the sun, standing very upright on three legs. "I have thought about it for a long time," it says. "Noon is mine. The solstice is yours. On that one day you may cross, once, and every rooster may crow, and I will pretend it is a courtesy. Agreed?"

choices.text: Agree, and bow

effects.log: You bow. The crow bows. Every rooster in the south crows at noon, on the solstice, from that year on, and the farmers call it the red hour and say it is lucky to be born in it. A truce between two proud birds is the warmest thing in the sky.

choices.text: Agree, and ask for one more day in winter

effects.log: "Winter?" says the crow. "Whatever for?" "The cold houses," you say. It looks at you a long time. "The winter solstice, then," it says. "One crossing. Low." On the longest night, every year after, the dawn comes a little warmer than it should.

choices.text: Refuse. Summer is not shared

effects.log: You refuse. The crow says nothing at all, and carries the sun on across noon, and you are left in the white glare holding your pride, which is very hot to hold. You cross on the solstice anyway. It does not stop you. It does not bow either. (-2 health)

events.text: You fly south over the sea past the last island anyone in the south has named, and on the night of the autumn equinox you see it: a star so low on the water that it seems to sit on the waves, red-white, the colour of a coal blown on. From the land it can be seen only from the southern island, and only on clear nights. On a black rock under it sits an old man with a forehead as high as a temple roof and a staff taller than he is.

choices.text: Land beside him and wait to be spoken to

effects.log: He does not speak for a long time. Then: "You are the warm one. From the north." Nobody has ever called the south north before. From down here it is. He offers you a peach. It is the best thing you have ever eaten.

choices.text: Ask him who he is

effects.log: "Old," he says. "Very old. I am the star of being old. Whoever sees me lives long; that is all I do." He looks up at his star, which is dimmer than it should be. "I am tired, warm one. That is all."

choices.text: Show off: flare until the sea is red

effects.log: The sea goes red to the horizon. The old man shades his eyes and laughs, a dry, kind sound. "Young," he says. "Very young. Good. Come back when you are tired too."

events.text: The southern island is giving a feast for its old: every islander past eighty at the long tables in the governor's yard, some past ninety, three past a hundred, and the governor counting them into a book because nobody in the capital will believe it. After dark the old ones go out on the sea wall and look south for the Old Man Star. Only a few of them can still see that far.

choices.text: Fly low over the sea wall and warm them while they look

effects.log: The night is cold off the sea and suddenly is not. The old ones stay out on the wall till midnight, pointing, arguing about which red light is the star. One of them is pointing at you. You let them think it.

choices.text: Fly south and blow on the star, so it shows

effects.log: You fly out to the black rock and breathe on the star like a coal, and it brightens, and on the sea wall every old face lifts at once. The old man on the rock looks at you sidelong. "Showing off again," he says, and then, "Thank you."

choices.text: Sit on the governor's roof and listen to them talk

effects.log: Long lives, it turns out, are mostly made of small things: fish, quarrels, the weather, a neighbour's dog. You listen until the lamps go out, and fly south with your head full of a hundred years of somebody else's weather.

events.text: In the capital the court has stopped the rite for the Old Man Star. It was a small rite, a minor sacrifice, the beast for it kept alive afterwards by the office of sacrifices, and a minister has said it is a waste. Out on his black rock the old man's star is dimmer this year, and his hands shake on the staff. "Nobody has thanked me for long life in a while," he says. "It is not the thanks. It is the being looked for."

choices.text: Carry him a coal of your own heart

effects.log: You open your breast feathers and take out a coal of yourself and set it in his star like a new wick. It brightens. On the southern island the old people say the star is back, and live, every one of them, a year longer than they expected. (-10 health)

choices.text: Fly to the capital and perch on the minister's roof

ok.log: You sit on his ridge-pole and tell him, quite politely, what the rite was for. He restores it in the spring, very quietly, under a different name, so as not to look as if a bird told him to.

fail.log: He calls the guard, the guard calls the archers, and you leave with the rite still stopped and the insult still in your throat.

choices.text: Sit with him a while instead

effects.log: You sit on the rock beside him all winter while the star burns low. He tells you about the people who have looked for him: fishermen, widows, an emperor once. You understand that he is not asking for help. He is asking for company, which is harder.

events.text: The old man is waiting for you on his black rock, and he has put down his staff. That has never happened. "Warm one," he says. "I have been the star of long life since before your mansions had names. I would like to be an old man for a while, and then nothing. The star needs a fire. You are a fire. Think about it. Not long. I am old."

choices.text: Say you will think about it

effects.log: He nods and picks the staff up again, for now. You fly north with the question under your wing. It does not get lighter.

choices.text: Say no, kindly: the south still needs you

effects.log: "Yes," he says, "that is what I said, too, to the one before me." He does not seem offended. He seems, if anything, relieved that you know what it costs.

choices.text: Ask what becomes of the one who takes the star

effects.log: "You stay low," he says. "Very low, on the edge of the world, seen only from one island. Whoever sees you lives long. That is all. It is enough. It is also everything else gone." He looks at you. "You will not see a summer from the inside again."

events.text: The Old Man Star is a coal at the bottom of the sky, almost out. On the black rock the old man sits with his eyes closed, his staff across his knees. On the southern island the old ones stand on the sea wall every clear night and cannot find it. "Now," he says, without opening his eyes, "or someone else. Or nobody."

choices.text: Blow on it once more and fly home

effects.log: You breathe on the star with everything you have, and it comes up red-white on the water, and on the sea wall someone shouts. "Stubborn," says the old man, and takes up his staff again. "Another century, then. For you." (-12 health)

choices.text: Find him another fire: the Lantern of your own ferry

effects.log: You bring him a coal from the Lantern, the fire that guides distant travellers home. It takes in the star like a seed in good soil. The old man laughs. "Clever," he says. "A lamp for the far ones. I should have thought of it." He keeps the staff.

choices.text: Take his staff, and become his fire

effects.log: You take the staff. It is very light. The old man stands up, stiffly, smiles at you once, and walks away across the water toward the edge of the world, getting smaller. You settle on the black rock and burn. Low, red-white, at the very bottom of the sky, seen only from one island, on clear nights. Whoever sees you lives long. You never see a summer from the inside again, and every old face on the sea wall is turned toward you.

events.text: The long patrol: once every summer you fly the southern sea from end to end, island to island, so that every harbour fire, every lighthouse lamp, every cooking fire on a fishing boat knows whose sea this is. The divers on the volcanic island come up from the water, push back their masks, and wave. They have waved at you for generations. Some of them think you are an ancestor.

choices.text: Fly low and warm the water where they dive

effects.log: A warm patch of sea all summer off the black rocks. The divers stay down longer and come up with more. The island never works out why that cove is warm, and calls it by your name, more or less.

choices.text: Fly high and count every harbour fire

effects.log: Four hundred and six. One more than last summer: a new village on a bare islet, three houses and a drying rack. You burn a little prouder all the way home, as if you had built it yourself.

choices.text: Race the sea wind from end to end

effects.log: You beat it by half a day. The wind arrives sulking at the last island and blows the drying fish off a rack. Somebody on the island shouts at the sky. You take that as a compliment.

events.text: A storm comes up off the southern sea on the patrol, black from water to sky, with a whole fishing fleet of forty boats caught in the open under it. The boats have lit their cooking fires to see by. Forty little fires, every one of them going out.

choices.text: Fly into the storm's heart and burn it hollow

ok.log: You go up through the cloud at full heat and the storm opens round you like a wet paper door. Under the hole in it the sea goes flat. Forty boats row home in a circle of sunshine in the middle of a gale, and forty crews swear to it for the rest of their lives.

fail.log: The storm is wetter than you are hot. It pours on you until you are dim as a coal in a puddle. The fleet comes home anyway, battered, all forty, steering by your light, which they took for a lantern on the headland. (-20 health)

choices.text: Light the forty cooking fires again, boat by boat

effects.log: Forty times down to the pitching decks, forty coals, forty fires. The crews see them, and see each other, and keep together, and row home in a line of little red lights. (-8 health)

choices.text: Perch on the headland and burn as a beacon

effects.log: You sit on the headland all night as bright as you can make yourself. The fleet steers for you. Thirty-eight come in. You do not know about the other two for a week, and then they come in too, from the wrong island, with a story.

events.text: Far out on the patrol, on an island cliff that has no business being cold, there is frost: white on the black rock in high summer, and under a crooked pine, two pale eyes watching you go by. Something has come a very long way from its own quarter of the world to see the sea. It does not move. It is the White Tiger of the west, and it is looking at you the way autumn looks at the end of summer: patiently.

choices.text: Dip a wing to it as you pass

effects.log: The eyes blink, slowly, once. That is all. But years later, at the council, the Tiger will tell somebody it met you over the southern sea, and you will know exactly which summer it means.

choices.text: Sing it one note, across the water

effects.log: One note. The frost on the cliff melts a hand's width in a perfect circle and freezes again. You take that for an answer. It is.

choices.text: Fly closer, hotter, to make it squint

effects.log: You come in low and burning, and the frost hisses off the cliff in a white cloud, and the pine catches at the top. When the steam clears the eyes are gone. A dog-day heat lingers on that island all autumn. (Ash +1)

events.text: The ninth month, and it is still summer. The persimmons hang green. The rice stands heavy and will not turn. The wells are a bucket-rope lower than the old marks, and the old people have begun to look south, at you, with the particular stillness of people who know whose fault a season is. You held the solstice too long. You have been holding it ever since.
events.arc: The Summer That Would Not End

choices.text: Let go now, all at once

effects.log: You open your wings and give the season away. That night the wind turns northwest and the persimmons redden in a week, as if they had been waiting with their breath held. The rice comes in late and light, and it comes in.

choices.text: Ask the barley whether it wants another month

effects.log: The barley does not answer, being barley. The rice droops. A grandmother at a dry well looks up at the sky and says, not loudly, "Enough, now." You hear it. You do not let go. Not quite yet.

choices.text: Hold it. Summer is good

effects.log: You hold it. The days stay long and gold. The children swim in the river in the tenth month. The old people stop looking at you and start looking west.

events.text: On the far ridge of the west, in the summer that will not end, there is frost. Only there: a rim of white along one ridge-line, as if somebody had drawn it with a brush. In a cave mouth under it, two cold blue lights. A letter comes on a north wind, written in the frost on a roof tile. It says, in the old courteous style of the four directions: The west would be grateful for the autumn.
events.arc: The Summer That Would Not End

choices.text: Send autumn west at once, with an apology

effects.log: You fold the summer and send it home, and with it a feather, singed at the tip, by way of sorry. The frost on the ridge comes down the mountain the next morning like a tide going out, and autumn is two weeks late and very handsome.

choices.text: Swallow the insult of being asked

effects.log: Asked. As if the south were a tenant. You hold your tongue and hold the summer, both, and both of them burn. (-2 health)

choices.text: Write back: the west can wait

effects.log: You burn your answer into the roof tile. It cracks. The frost on the ridge does not move, and the two blue lights do not blink, and somewhere in the south a rice field goes brown overnight. (Ash +1)

events.text: A rain rite in a dry county in what should be the tenth month. The village has made a bird of straw and red rag, a long-tailed bird with a crest, and set it up on a pole in the dry paddy, and the children are beating it with sticks and singing for rain. You are the villain of the song. It is a good song. You know the tune.
events.arc: The Summer That Would Not End

choices.text: Let go, here, in front of the children

effects.log: You let go of the summer while the straw bird is still on its pole. The wind turns. Clouds come up from the west by evening. It rains for three days and the children dance in it round a sodden straw bird, and you watch from a far ridge, wet, and not unhappy.

choices.text: Hold on, and sing the rain song with them, very quietly

effects.log: You sing your own villain's song under your breath from the pine above the paddy, and hold the summer anyway, because letting go is the hardest thing a fire does. (-2 health)

choices.text: Burn the straw bird where it stands

effects.log: It goes up in one breath. So does the pole, and the dry stubble round it, and the edge of the threshing floor. The children run. Nobody is hurt. Nobody in that county ever sings that song kindly again. (Ash +1)

events.text: The White Tiger comes down. Not to the council: to the south, to the brown paddies and the dry wells, walking through your summer with frost forming in its footprints. It stops in the middle of a withered field and looks up at you, and does not roar. "Give it to me," it says. "Autumn. Now. Or I take it."
events.arc: The Summer That Would Not End

choices.text: Give it, and bow

effects.log: You come down into the field and bow to the White Tiger, beak to the cracked earth. The summer goes out of you like breath. It is the hardest thing you have ever done. The Tiger looks at you a long time and then, gravely, bows back, and autumn comes in behind it, cool and gold.

choices.text: Fight it for the season

ok.log: You drive it back up the western ridge in a storm of fire and frost, and win, and the summer is yours, and the rice is dead. You stand in the brown field afterwards and understand that winning was the wrong thing. You let a little of the summer go, enough for a late, thin harvest.

fail.log: It takes autumn from you the way autumn takes a leaf: without hurry, without mercy, all at once. You lie in the field with your feathers frosted. The persimmons redden overnight. (-25 health)

choices.text: Keep the summer. Let it take what it can

effects.log: You keep it. The harvest withers to the root, the wells go dry, and the White Tiger comes on through the south with autumn behind it like a tide, and you burn and burn against it, and lose. When the first frost reaches you, there is nothing left in the south that is warm, and you are not either.

events.text: There is a county in the south where the swallows did not come back this spring. Not one. On the third of the third month the old people stood in their yards with their faces turned up, and the eaves stayed empty, and the nests from last year hung there grey and dry. The hills round the county are black. You remember why. Every fire that ran, every temper let out: it is all here, in one place, looking at you.

choices.text: Fly the black hills slowly, and look at all of it

effects.log: It takes a month. You make yourself see every slope, every blackened stump, every house rebuilt in a hurry. Ash cannot be unburned. It can be looked at. That is the only thing you can do with it, and you do it.

choices.text: Plant fire-field millet on the black slopes with the farmers

effects.log: Burnt ground grows millet, the fire-field people say. You help them sow it, the bird who burned it, walking the furrows like a hen. By autumn the black hills have a green fuzz on them. The swallows still do not come. (-6 health)

choices.text: Fly away and do not look back

effects.log: You fly away. The black county stays exactly where it is. You find that you carry it, after, somewhere under your breast feathers, hot and heavy as a swallowed coal. (-2 health)

events.text: A dry spring wind, and a fire that is not yours, a charcoal-burner's kiln left open, gets loose in the black county and runs up the first slope. The people do not run to put it out. They stand in the road and look up at you, every one, because in this county every fire is yours, whoever lit it.

choices.text: Come down into it and take it into your breast

ok.log: You swallow it, slope by slope, the whole fire, until there is nothing left on the hill but smoke and a red bird lying in it, panting. The people in the road do not cheer. They go home. One old woman leaves a bowl of water on a stone for you.

fail.log: There is too much of it. You take half and the wind takes the rest over the ridge. It is not your fire. It is your ash. (Ash +1, -20 health)

choices.text: Beat it out with your wings, the way the villagers would

effects.log: You come down and beat at it with your wings like a farmer with a wet sack, and after a moment the farmers come up the slope and beat beside you. It goes out by evening. Nobody says anything. It is the first time in that county anyone has stood next to you. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let it burn. It is not yours

effects.log: You do not move. It burns the slope and the next. The people in the road watch you not move. In that county, now, there is no difference between the fires you lit and the fires you watched. (Ash +1)

events.text: It begins in the black county and does not stay there. A dry year, a wind out of the southwest, and the old ash of everything you ever let run catches again, all of it at once, mountain after mountain. You feel it in your breast like a second heart. This is the fire your whole record has been leaning toward. It is asking whether you will be it.

choices.text: Fly into the front of it and hold it with your body

effects.log: You spread yourself across the head of the fire like a firebreak made of feathers and hold it on one ridge for nine days. It goes out against you. You come back grey to the shoulders and do not burn properly for a decade. The swallows do not come back to that county. They come back to the next. (-30 health)

choices.text: Go east and beg the Azure Dragon for rain

effects.log: You fly to the east and bow on the dragon's ridge, fire to water, which costs you more than any fight. The rain comes for three days. The fire drowns. The dragon says only, "You came yourself. Good." (-10 health)

choices.text: Let it run. Be the fire you made

effects.log: You stop holding. The fire goes over one mountain and the next and the next, and you go with it, because it is you, it was always you, every fire you let run and every temper you let out. It does not stop at the edge of the south. The swallows do not come back. When it is over, there is a burned country the length of the coast, and a name for it, and the name is yours.

events.text: Twenty years and more, and not one fire of yours burning anywhere in the world. You did not notice it happening: a fire out here, a keeper dead there, a slope called home, a long sleep. Now your feathers are grey at the tips, the way they were when you were a chick in the ash, and on cold mornings you are slow to rise. Summer came three weeks late this year. People are talking about it.

choices.text: Give a fire now, the first cold house you find

effects.log: A cold house at the end of a mountain village, a child with chilblains, a dead stove. Your coal is small and grey and you are ashamed of it. It takes anyway. The grey goes out of your wingtips by spring. (The Hearth burns.)

choices.text: Light a Field Fire on a slope that needs one

effects.log: A fire-field family on a steep slope, the old fire cold three seasons. You give them a coal and they burn the slope in the old way, and the millet comes, and the grey in your wingtips turns, slowly, red. (The Field Fire burns.)

choices.text: Sit where you are. You are tired

effects.log: You sit. Grey is a restful colour. Somewhere a house is cold that need not be, and somewhere else another, and you know it, the way you know your own heartbeat, which is slower than it was.

events.text: You find yourself, without meaning to, in a ruined house in the south: the roof half in, a persimmon tree growing through the kitchen floor, and on the floor, a clay fire jar, cold. It is not the jar you were born in. It is exactly the shape of it. You sit on its lip for a long time. It would be very easy to get in.

choices.text: Get up and fly to the nearest lit window

effects.log: A ferry-landing a valley over, its lantern long dark, a ferry-keeper who still rows at night out of habit. You put a coal in the lantern. The ferry-keeper looks up at it and starts to cry, for no reason they can name. (The Lantern burns.)

choices.text: Warm the jar, a little, for whoever comes next

effects.log: You breathe into the jar until the clay is warm. Then you leave it. Some traveller sheltering here this winter will find a warm jar in a cold house and not know why, and live.

choices.text: Look at it a while longer

effects.log: You look. The jar looks back, the way jars do. It is still there when you leave. You will remember the way.

events.text: Winter, and you are in the ruined house again, and you do not remember flying here. Snow comes in through the broken roof and lies on the cold jar, and does not melt on you. You are nearly all grey now. Summer came six weeks late everywhere in the south this year. The jar is open. It is very quiet in there.

choices.text: Rise, and give one fire, any fire, before you rest

effects.log: You rise. It takes everything. You fly through the snow to the first cold kitchen you find and drop a coal into it, grey, hardly warm, and it catches, and a child in a padded jacket kneels and blows on it. The grey in you stops spreading. (The Hearth burns.) (-10 health)

choices.text: Fly south to the kilns and lie in the warm ash a while

effects.log: You go south to an old celadon kiln and lie in its warm ash all winter, and in spring you are a little redder, enough to fly. It is not a fire given. It is a fire borrowed. It will do, for now.

choices.text: Get into the cold jar, and stay

effects.log: You get in. The clay is cold all round you, and quiet, and grey, and so are you. The snow fills the jar slowly and does not melt. Summer comes late everywhere that year, and the next, and every year after, and nobody in the south remembers that it used to come on time.

events.text: The cinnabar hunters have a master now. {npc} has ground every red feather the south ever dropped into ink, and the talismans written in it work, and {he} has decided that a feather is a waste when there is a whole bird. On the beacon roads, at the kiln villages, by the ferries, there are notices on the gates: a reward, very large, for the red bird, alive.

choices.text: Go quiet. Fly only at night for a while

effects.log: You fly by night and sleep in chimneys. The notices fade in the rain. {npc} does not take them down. {He} prints more.

choices.text: Perch on {his} roof and look at {him} through the window

effects.log: {npc} looks up from the mortar and sees you on the ridge tiles, red against the dusk, and does not look away. Neither do you. {He} raises the pestle to you, slowly, like a cup. It is the most frightening courtesy you have ever been paid.

choices.text: Burn every notice off every gate in one night

effects.log: Three hundred notices, three hundred gates, one night. Some of the gates catch. By morning the south knows exactly where you were, gate by gate, and {npc} draws the line of them on a map and smiles. (Ash +1)

events.text: {npc} has built a mortar for you. You see it from the air: a great stone bowl the size of a well-head in a walled yard in the hills, polished smooth inside, and beside it, coiled like a sleeping snake, a net of iron chain that is kept soaking in river water so it will not heat. {He} has thought about this for a long time.

choices.text: Steal the net and drop it in the sea

ok.log: It is very heavy and very wet and you get it to the coast just before dawn and let it go into the deep. {npc} comes out into the yard, finds the empty tub, and laughs. {He} starts on another net that afternoon.

fail.log: The chain is cold and wet and drags you down onto the yard stones. You get away. The net does not. {npc} watches from the door and makes a note. (-14 health)

choices.text: Remember the ink a human once made of your feather

effects.log: A feather of yours carried to a sect elder in a box long ago, by someone who had to choose. The ink was red and the talismans worked and a hungry ghost went away from a gate because of it. It was not all bad, the mortar. You look at this one a long time.

choices.text: Crack the mortar with heat

effects.log: You sit on the rim and burn until the stone rings and splits from top to bottom. The yard catches. Nobody is hurt. {npc} looks at the two halves of the mortar for a long time and then orders a new one, bigger. (Ash +1)

events.text: The net comes down at the kiln village at dusk: iron chain, soaked, a hundred hired men on the ropes, and {npc} at the back with a lantern, not hurrying. You were warming a potter's firebox. You are on the ground in the wet cold weight of it before you know what it is.

choices.text: Burst it

ok.log: You go white-hot inside the chain until the water in it screams into steam and the links go soft, and you come up through the net like a fire through a straw roof. The hired men drop the ropes. {npc} does not drop the lantern. "Next time," {he} says.

fail.log: The chain holds. You get one wing free and drag yourself out under the edge, leaving feathers in it, a whole handful. {npc} gathers them up carefully, one by one, by lantern light. (-25 health)

choices.text: Go still and cold under it, until they think you dead

ok.log: You go grey and still as old ash. The men lift the net to look. You are gone up the potter's chimney before the first of them shouts.

fail.log: {npc} is not fooled. {He} has the men pile wet sacks on the net and you lie under them all night before the potter, at dawn, cuts the ropes and runs. (-18 health)

choices.text: Burn the whole village round the net

effects.log: Everything goes up: the ropes, the men's sleeves, the potter's drying racks, two houses. You come up out of the fire free. The village does not forgive you. Neither, oddly, does {npc}, who wanted you whole. (Ash +2)

events.text: This time the net holds. You lie in the walled yard in the hills beside the great stone mortar, iron chain over every feather, and {npc} sits on the rim of the mortar with the pestle across {his} knees, old now, patient. "Every talisman in the south," {he} says, "for a thousand years. Against fever, ghosts, fire. Written in you. Think what good you would do."

choices.text: Burst the chain with everything you have

ok.log: Everything. The chain goes soft as noodles and the mortar cracks in half and you are in the air. {npc} sits on in the ruined yard with the pestle across {his} knees and watches you go, and does not call the men, and you understand that {he} is too old to try again.

fail.log: The chain holds, and holds, and you burn yourself grey against it, and at dawn the potter of the kiln village comes over the wall with an axe and cuts one link and runs. You owe a potter your life. (-30 health)

choices.text: Offer {him} a feather, freely given, every year

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it for a whole night, sitting on the mortar. "Freely given," {he} says at dawn, "writes better." {He} lets you go. Every year after, on the first day of summer, there is a red feather on the rim of the mortar. The talismans of the south are very good that century.

choices.text: Stop struggling. Let the mortar have you

effects.log: You stop. {npc} is very gentle about it, which is the worst part. Your feathers go into the mortar one by one and come out as ink, a red so bright it hurts, and for a thousand years every talisman written in the south is written in you, against fever and ghosts and fire, and they work. Nobody who uses them knows that the ink was once a bird who gave fire to a widow's cold kitchen.

events.text: An envoy of the Jade court has come down to read the south its own record, aloud, in the archive of heaven, a hall of shelves that goes up into cloud. The envoy reads well and slowly, and mispronounces the name of your first keeper, and then the name of your kiln, and then calls the Southern Palace "the warm quarter" as if it were a district of a market town. Under your breast feathers everything you ever swallowed turns over.

choices.text: Sing it out, right here, before it flares

effects.log: You sing over the envoy's reading, a counter-melody, every name pronounced properly, loud. The clerks stop writing. The envoy, to their credit, stops too, and listens, and starts again from the beginning, correctly. The heat in you goes down to embers. Embers is still heat.

choices.text: Swallow it, again

effects.log: You clamp your beak shut and swallow it. And the next one. And the one after. By the end of the reading the shelf you are sitting on is warm enough to cook rice on, and the scroll beside you has gone brown at the edges. Nobody notices. Yet. (-2 health)

choices.text: Let one laugh out, a small one

effects.log: A small laugh. A very small one. It sets three scrolls on the bottom shelf alight and the envoy's sleeve, and the clerks beat them out with their ledgers. "The south," says the envoy, very evenly, "is reminded where it is." (Ash +1)

events.text: The envoy is back, and has brought the whole of the south's record from the archive of heaven: nine halls of it, every year of you since the fire jar, every warm house and every wildfire. It will be read aloud, from the beginning. It will take nine days. The envoy has been warned about you, and has brought a bucket.

choices.text: Sing for nine days and nights, to keep the heat moving

effects.log: Nine days. You sing under the reading the whole time, and the heat in you goes out into the song and up into the cloud, and the bucket is never needed. On the ninth day the envoy closes the last scroll and looks at you with something like respect. "Long," the envoy says. "Hot. Mostly honest."

choices.text: Leave the archive before the reading starts

effects.log: You go. Rudeness is ash of a kind, but a smaller kind than what was coming. Behind you in the archive the envoy reads for nine days to an empty perch, and writes in the margin: the south declined to attend. (-6 health)

choices.text: Stay, and hold it in

effects.log: You stay and hold it in for nine days. On the ninth, as the envoy reaches the last page, the bucket begins to steam on its own. The envoy notices that. The envoy says nothing, and you are almost grateful. (-2 health)

events.text: The audit in the archive of heaven, the last day, and the envoy finishes the south's record, rolls up the scroll, and says one word too many. It is not even a rude word. It is "pheasant". Everything you ever swallowed, every insult, every grief, every great joy you sat on because it was not seemly, comes up your throat all at once, and it is not fire. It is laughter.

choices.text: Sing it, all of it, now, and let the song take it

effects.log: You turn the laugh into a song half a breath before it leaves you, and it goes up into the clouds instead of along the shelves, a song so long and so loud that every swallow in the south hears it and sings back. When it ends you are cool for the first time in a century. The envoy has taken out a handkerchief.

choices.text: Fly out through the roof of heaven before it comes

effects.log: You go up through the archive roof and out into the open sky and laugh there, where there is nothing to burn but cloud. The cloud burns anyway, a little, red at the edges, all evening. (Ash +1, -15 health)

choices.text: Laugh

effects.log: You laugh. It comes out of you like summer through a paper door. The scroll in the envoy's hand goes first, and then the shelf, and then the hall, and the archive of heaven burns for nine days, every record of every guardian, yours first. When it is over the Jade court sends you down as one spark, and every record of you is ash, and somewhere a fire jar on the coldest night has a little red point in it that will not stop chirping.

events.text: You go up from the south in a column of heat, the way, you will learn, you always will, and come out onto the council terrace among the stars. They are all there before you. In the north the Black Tortoise with its serpent, both heads talking at once. In the east the Azure Dragon, long as a mountain range, and in the west the White Tiger with stars in its stripes, seated, both far older than you. In the centre a gold light that may be the Yellow Dragon pretending to sleep. "The youngest," says the tortoise. "Bows first," says the serpent. "To everyone," they finish together.

choices.text: Bow to each of them in turn, first and low

effects.log: North, east, west, centre, beak to the cloud each time, slowly, the way the south bows at a rite. Each of them bows back, the Tiger last and lowest. The serpent says it has seen better bows. The tortoise says from whom. You understand that this is how the north does everything, and that bowing first costs less than you thought, and is worth more.

choices.text: Bow to all four at once, turning on the spot

effects.log: You spin on the terrace bowing, north east west centre, so fast your tail sets a little cloud smouldering. The Azure Dragon makes a sound like a river under ice, which you realise later was laughing. The tortoise writes it down as one bow. The serpent writes it down as four.

choices.text: Refuse. The south goes in front; the Book of Rites says so

effects.log: You do not bow. "In front, the vermilion bird," you quote. "Behind, the dark warrior." The tortoise says, "In front means you face the enemy first, not that you are served first." The serpent says nothing at all. It is a long, hot afternoon, and the thing you did not do sits in your throat like a coal. (-2 health)

events.text: The Black Tortoise reads your record aloud before the council, plate by plate, slowly. It is your life as the north wrote it down from far off: the fires given, the fires that ran, the tempers. Halfway through it reads a line someone wrote long ago about the south: "A hot wind and a nuisance; sets things alight when amused."

choices.text: Correct it, politely, with dates

effects.log: You give the year of every fire, the name of every keeper. The tortoise amends the plate. The serpent reads the amendment and says, "It is still a nuisance." "Yes," you agree. "But a precise one." Even the Tiger laughs.

choices.text: Swallow it. It is a little true

effects.log: It is a little true. You sit very still and let the tortoise read on, and the line stays on the shell, and in you. (-2 health)

choices.text: Burn that line off the shell. Only that line

effects.log: One line, very neatly, a little smoke. The tortoise looks at the blackened place on its plate for a long time. "Now it is true," says the serpent, "and also gone." That, you will learn, is the trouble with records. (Ash +1)

events.text: "The north reads," says the tortoise. "The south sings," says the serpent. "So sing it," they say together. "Your record. The warmth and the ash. Do not skip the ugly verses." The whole council turns toward you. The Yellow Dragon in the centre opens one eye. Somewhere far below, every fire you ever gave is burning, or is not.

choices.text: Sing all of it: every fire given, every fire that ran

effects.log: You sing the widow's kitchen and the kiln and the beacon and the ferry lantern, and then, without stopping, every slope that burned, every temper, every keeper who died in a fire you forgot. Your voice does not go soft on the ugly verses; it goes hot. When you finish nobody speaks for a long time. The Tortoise stops writing to listen, and then writes one word.

choices.text: Sing the warm verses, beautifully, and leave the rest

effects.log: It is the most beautiful thing the council has heard in an age, and every guardian on the terrace knows exactly what you left out. The tortoise writes, in small characters, under your song: incomplete. "Come back," says the serpent, not unkindly, "when you can sing the rest."

choices.text: Ask for time to make the song

effects.log: "A song of a life is not made in an afternoon," you say. The serpent says, "Good," as if you had passed something. The tortoise says, "We will wait." It is the north. It is very good at waiting.

events.text: The council has not heard you sing the whole of your record yet, and the south seat stays empty while it waits. The tortoise sends a note south on a cold wind, very short: Whenever you are ready. The serpent has added under it, in a smaller hand: The ugly verses are the ones we need.

choices.text: Go up now and sing all of it

effects.log: You go up in a column of heat and sing it, the whole of it, the warm verses and the ugly ones, and you do not look away from any of the four while you do it. At the end the Tiger, of all of them, bows to you first. You will remember that.

choices.text: Not yet. Some of the verses are still burning

effects.log: You stay in the south. Some of what you would have to sing is still happening, on slopes and in houses, and you go and see to it first. The note from the north you keep in your breast feathers. It does not burn.

events.text: A sitting of the council, and the Azure Dragon and you both rise to bow to each other at the same moment, out of pure good manners, and bang heads, gently, in the middle of the terrace. There is a short silence. Then something in you that has been swallowed for a very long time comes up, and it is a laugh.

choices.text: Swallow the laugh, for dignity

effects.log: You hold it in. Your eyes water sparks. The dragon, who is also holding it in, looks at you, and you both look away very fast. The council goes on. It is the longest afternoon of your life. (-2 health)

choices.text: Turn it into a song before it catches

effects.log: You sing it instead, a little rising tune about two very old, very dignified creatures and one very small forehead. The dragon hums the low part. The tortoise's record stays unburnt, this time. The serpent looks almost disappointed.

choices.text: Laugh

effects.log: You laugh so hard that you set fire to the Black Tortoise's record, the plate it was reading from, and the serpent has to put it out with its own coils, hissing, and the council is adjourned for a day. The dragon, rubbing its head, is laughing too. The tortoise is not. The tortoise writes it down, later, with the date. (Ash +1)

events.text: A witness is called before the council: {npc}, a human of the high heavens, who once sat at your table in the Southern Palace and raised a cup to the empty seat before sitting down, the seat of the guest who burned. {He} stands before the four directions and says, "I was a guest of the south. It fed me. I would like that written."

choices.text: Rise and bow to {him} first, before {he} can bow to you

effects.log: You come down off the south seat and bow to {npc}, a guardian to a guest, beak to the cloud, in front of the whole council. The tortoise stops writing. "That," says the serpent, "is the south." {npc} bows back, and weeps, and the Yellow Dragon pretends very hard to be asleep.

choices.text: Let {him} tell it, every dish

effects.log: {npc} tells the whole banquet: the solstice noon, the seven mansions as one bird, the kitchen of the Extended Net, the empty seat. The Tiger asks what the soup was. {npc} remembers. The tortoise writes the soup down.

events.text: A witness is called before the council: {npc}, a human of the high heavens, who once sat down uninvited in the scorched seat at your table in the Southern Palace, the seat of the guest who burned. {He} has a faint red print on {his} robe that never washed out. "I sat in it," {he} tells the four directions. "Rude or brave. The south never told me which."

choices.text: Tell {him}: both. That is why it was allowed

effects.log: "Both," you say. "In the south it is often the same thing." {npc} laughs out loud before the council, which nobody does. The Tiger looks at {him} with real approval. The tortoise writes: both.

choices.text: Ask {him} to sit in the south seat for a moment, to see

effects.log: The serpent hisses. The tortoise says nothing. {npc} sits in the south seat of the sky for the space of one breath, very straight, very hot, and gets up again with a second red print on the robe. The Yellow Dragon opens both eyes. It is, everyone agrees later, the most improper moment in the history of the council.

events.text: A witness is called before the council: {npc}, a human of the high heavens, who once sang for {his} place at your table in the Southern Palace, an old harvest song from {his} village, off-key, with a verse about a drunk uncle. "The south gave me the seat beside its wing," {he} says. "I was asked to say what the south is like. I can only sing it."

choices.text: Sing the harmony under {him}, as you did

effects.log: {npc} sings the harvest song and you sing under it like heat off a summer road. Halfway through, the Azure Dragon starts to beat time on the terrace with its tail. The tortoise writes the words. The serpent writes the tune. The drunk uncle enters the record of heaven for ever.

choices.text: Let {him} sing it alone

effects.log: A human voice alone on the terrace of the four directions, a little off-key. It is, you realise, the most honest record of the south anyone has ever given. Nobody burns anything.

events.text: The White Tiger comes over to your side of the terrace after a sitting, which it has never done, and lies down a careful distance from the heat. "They will ask me about you," it says, "when the south seat is filled. Tell me something true, so I know what to say."

choices.text: "You saw me once, over the southern sea"

effects.log: "The patrol," says the Tiger. "The island with the frost. You dipped your wing." It is quiet a while. "I will say you are courteous," it says, "when it costs you nothing, and sometimes when it does."

choices.text: "In the dog days I leave your cave alone"

effects.log: "You stand outside it and talk," says the Tiger. "For hours. About weather." It considers. "I will say you know when to stay outside a door." From the Tiger, that is a great deal.

choices.text: "I am afraid of how much I like summer"

effects.log: The Tiger looks at you for a long time. "Good," it says at last. "So am I, of autumn." It does not say anything else. It does not need to.

choices.text: "I am the fire. That is the truth"

effects.log: "That is not a truth," says the Tiger. "That is a birth." It gets up and goes back to the west. You do not understand what it meant for a century, and then you do, all at once, on a slope you had let burn.

events.text: You take your place in the south of the council, and for the first time in your life the circle is closed around you: the black north, the azure east, the white west, and you, burning, in front. In the centre the gold light gathers into the Yellow Dragon of the middle, of earth and of the late summer between all seasons. It looks at you with the patience of farmland. "The record is sung," it says. "Now tell me what you will do with summer."

choices.text: "Give it away. Every year, to every cold house"

effects.log: "Then give it," says the Yellow Dragon, as if that settled everything, and it does. The north writes it on the shell. The west nods once. In the east the dragon lets out a breath like rain on hot stone.

choices.text: "Keep every fire I gave, and not let one run"

effects.log: "Not one?" says the Yellow Dragon. "That is a great deal to promise." "Then I will promise less and do more," you say. The serpent laughs, a dry crack like river ice. The tortoise writes both versions down.

choices.text: "I do not know yet. I will learn it from the kitchens"

effects.log: "Good," says the Yellow Dragon. "The ones who know already are the ones we have to replace." The council does not end. It simply begins, and you are part of it, and you sing one note to mark it, because the south always does.

choices.text: "Summer is mine. I will hold it as long as I like"

effects.log: The centre does not argue. It never argues. It only goes on looking at you with the patience of farmland, which outlasts every drought. Across the terrace, in the west, the White Tiger is very still.

events.text: A quarrel in the council. The north wants a hard early frost for the locust eggs; the east wants a wet spring; the west wants an early autumn for its orchards. And the south, which is you, wants a long hot summer for the rice, and will say so, loudly. The Yellow Dragon in the middle has declined to have an opinion and is pretending to sleep.

choices.text: Fight the Tiger for the last week of summer

effects.log: The fight is spectacular and lasts a week. The weather that year is very strange: hail in the south, a heat wave in the west, a rainbow at midnight. Every guardian learns something about the others, and the Yellow Dragon, who was not asleep at all, writes it down.

choices.text: Give up a week of summer for the north's frost

effects.log: You end the summer a week early. The frost kills every locust egg in three provinces. The rice is a little short and nobody starves. The tortoise sends you a note that says only: Neat.

choices.text: Sing the case for the rice until they all give in

ok.log: You sing the rice: the planting, the weeding, the wading women, the bowls. By the end the Tiger is looking at its paws. You get your long summer. The harvest is enormous. The locusts are a problem the next year, which is also, the tortoise points out, a record.

fail.log: You sing the rice. The serpent sings back the locusts, every verse, in a dry little voice, and wins. You go home with a short summer and a long temper.

events.text: A human comes up to the council terrace to testify, a proud immortal of the upper heavens, and stands before the four directions with {his} chin up and does not bow. {He} is waiting to be bowed to. Everybody looks at you. You are, after all, the one who knows about bowing first.

choices.text: Tell {him} what the north told you, word for word

effects.log: "The youngest," you say, "bows first. To everyone. I did. It cost less than I thought and was worth more." {npc} goes red to the ears, and bows, very low, to every quarter, and to you last. The serpent says it has seen better bows. The tortoise says from whom. You find you are enjoying yourself.

choices.text: Bow to {him} first, and see what {he} does

effects.log: You bow, guardian to human, first and low. {npc} is so astonished that {he} bows back lower than anyone has ever bowed on that terrace, and stays down, and has to be helped up by the serpent. Manners, you think, are a kind of fire. You give them away and they warm the other one.

choices.text: Say to {him}: "I am smaller than you, and younger, and I have done much less. Bow"

effects.log: It is not true, any of it, and {npc} knows it, and bows. You will say it again, centuries later, to someone much larger, and it will be no truer, and it will work.

events.text: The youngest seat keeps the minutes, the tortoise informs you, until the north can be spared to do it, which is never. A brush, an inkstone, a stack of paper. You write the first sitting down: what each guardian said. Spring said it was humble. Autumn said it was fair. You said you were kind. You read it back. It is all a little untrue, and you are the one who wrote it.

choices.text: Burn it. A false record is worse than none

effects.log: You hold the page in your beak until it catches, and let the ash go up into the stars. It feels better than anything you have done in a century. You burn the next sitting's minutes too. And the next. You keep the minutes, the council will say for ever after, very badly. You burn them, mostly.

choices.text: Write them true: what each said, and what each meant

effects.log: Spring said humble and meant afraid. Autumn said fair and meant hungry. You said kind and meant lonely. You write all of it. Nobody can bear to read it, least of all you. You keep it in a box. The box gets very warm.

choices.text: Sing them instead of writing them

effects.log: A sung record cannot be read back, only remembered, and everyone remembers it a little differently, which is, you think, closer to the truth. The tortoise disapproves. The serpent hums it for a week.

events.text: The serpent of the north finds you on the edge of the terrace, burning the minutes of the last sitting, page by page, and watches the ash go up for a while. "Why," it asks, "do the minutes always burn?"

choices.text: "Because nobody writes them true"

effects.log: "And a false record is worse than none," you say. The serpent thinks about that for a whole season. "One day," it says, "somebody slow will write them true." "Then I will stop," you say. Neither of you believes the other.

choices.text: "Because I like the colour of it"

effects.log: The serpent laughs, a dry crack like ice on a river, and coils round the tortoise's shell to tell it. The tortoise does not laugh. The tortoise, you suspect, writes down that you said it.

choices.text: Stop, and give the serpent the last page unburnt

effects.log: The serpent takes it carefully in its mouth and carries it north. It is the first page of the council's minutes to survive in an age. It says, in your hand, that the south was kind. The serpent writes under it: and lonely.

events.text: A whole century of minutes in a heap on the south edge of the terrace, scorched at the corners, waiting for you to finish burning them. You find you cannot. Somewhere below, perhaps not yet born, there is somebody slow enough and stubborn enough to write the council down true, the lies and what the lies meant. You do not know who. You would like to leave them something.

choices.text: Leave the heap unburnt, for whoever comes

effects.log: You leave it. It sits on the terrace through a hundred sittings, gathering frost on the north side. The tortoise looks at it now and then the way a farmer looks at a field nobody has sown yet.

choices.text: Burn it, and tell yourself you will stop next century

effects.log: It goes up in one breath. The ash rises into the stars and you watch it go with a sigh of relief that you are a little ashamed of. Next century, you tell yourself. You have been telling yourself that for a while.

events.text: An envoy of the Jade court arrives at the council terrace with a retinue of clerks and a mandate to audit the four guardians: winds, rains, harvests, verdicts, every century accounted for. The tortoise produces its shell. The Tiger lays a fine red deer at the envoy's feet, which is not what was asked for. The envoy turns, a little wearily, to the south.

choices.text: Produce a song

effects.log: Every fire, every keeper, every summer, by year, in verse, with a refrain. The clerks put down their brushes after the first century and simply listen. The envoy, at the end, says: "The south is in order," and then, after a pause, "Again, please, from the kiln."

choices.text: Recite every fire by year instead, to show you can

ok.log: Nine days, not one year missed. The clerks run out of ink twice. Afterwards the Azure Dragon tries to do its rains the same way and loses count in the third century, and you do not let it forget that for an age.

fail.log: You lose count somewhere around the third beacon and the envoy notes it, kindly, in red. The Tiger, who brought a deer, looks at you with enormous sympathy, which is worse.

choices.text: Laugh at the deer

effects.log: You laugh. The envoy's ledger catches at one corner, and the clerks beat it out, and the Black Tortoise laughs out loud with both heads, which nobody has heard before. The audit never quite recovers its dignity. (Ash +1)

events.text: The envoy is auditing the west and has come to the White Tiger's ghosts: how many were made, how many laid to rest, where the cairns are. The clerks have a separate ledger for it, bound in white hemp. The Tiger, asked for its records, has said only that the ledger is in the bird's song. The envoy sends for you.

choices.text: Sing the Tiger's ghosts, every name

effects.log: You sing each one a little softer than the last, the names and the villages and the roads. It takes three years. The clerks agree afterwards that it was the most beautiful audit in the history of the Jade court. The Tiger listens to every verse and does not look away once.

choices.text: Make the Tiger sing them with you

effects.log: The Tiger has a voice like a rockfall a long way off and cannot hold a note. It sings anyway, every name, under yours. The envoy writes nothing at all for the whole of it, and at the end closes the white ledger and says, "Received."

events.text: The audit is concluded. The envoy is packing the ledgers. The Azure Dragon, who has waited a decade for its chance, asks very politely who audits the Jade court. The envoy goes very still. The clerks stop packing. You can feel a laugh coming up through you like a fire up a chimney.

choices.text: Hold it in, for the envoy's sake

effects.log: You hold it. The envoy, who knows exactly what you are holding, bows to you on the way out, very slightly. That is worth something. It is also stuck in your throat for a decade. (-2 health)

choices.text: Answer for the envoy: "The song does"

effects.log: "The song does," you say. "Everyone remembers it differently. Even the Jade court." The envoy looks at you a long time, and then, to everyone's surprise, hums the refrain from the kiln all the way down the sky.

choices.text: Let it out

effects.log: You laugh. The envoy's hat catches. The Black Tortoise laughs with both heads, and the dragon looks delighted to have an accomplice, and the audit is concluded an hour early. (Ash +1)

events.text: A painter has come south from the old kingdom of the north with a box of pigments on {his} back and a commission from a dying king: a guardian for the door of the dark. {npc} has been sitting on a red-rock peak in the hills for a month, waiting, and when you come down at noon to see who is so patient, {he} does not run. {He} gets out a brush.

choices.text: Hold still on the peak and let {him} draw

effects.log: You hold still for a whole afternoon, which for you is very hard. {npc} draws fast, a hundred sketches, wings, tail, the turn of your head. At sunset {he} holds one up. It is you at the instant before flight. You have never seen that instant from outside.

choices.text: Show off: rise, turn, rise again

effects.log: You take off and land and take off, tail curling like a whirlwind each time. {npc} draws until {his} hand cramps and then draws with the other one. "Again," {he} keeps saying. "Again. No, the moment before."

choices.text: Ask {him} what a guardian of the dark is for

effects.log: "To stand by the door," says {npc}, "facing in, so the dead are not alone, and facing out, so nothing else comes in. The blue one on the east is done, and the white one on the west. The south wall is empty. The king wants the south to be the last thing in the dark."

events.text: {npc} has taken you north, to the tomb: a stone chamber under an earth mound, the walls plastered with lime, and by lamplight a blue dragon on the east wall and a white tiger on the west, both so alive that you flare a little at them out of habit. The south wall has a doorway in the middle of it. "You go here," says {npc}. "Twice. Once each side. Facing each other across the door."

choices.text: Ask why twice

effects.log: "Because the dead go out between you," says {npc}, grinding red. "And a guardian who is only on one side of a door is only half a guardian." You look at the doorway a long time. You have never been on both sides of anything.

choices.text: Bring {him} a lotus bud from the southern ponds

effects.log: You fly south and back in a night with a lotus bud in your beak, still closed, still wet. {npc} looks at it and at you and then paints the bud first, in your beak, before anything else, as if that were the important part.

choices.text: Refuse to be two. There is only one of you

effects.log: "There is one bird of the south," you say. {npc} nods and keeps grinding. "Then be one bird on two sides of a door," {he} says. "It is the same thing, to the dead." You sit on the lip of the doorway all night, hot and unconvinced. (-2 health)

events.text: The king of the north is dead and the tomb will be sealed in nine days. {npc} is old now, and works by one oil lamp on a ladder, slowly, and the south wall is nearly finished: on each side of the doorway a vermilion bird on red-brown peaks, wings raised at the instant of flight, tail curled like a whirlwind, a lotus bud in the beak. They face each other. They are both you. The eyes are not done.

choices.text: Hold the lamp for {him} while {he} paints the eyes

effects.log: You burn steady as a lamp for nine nights while {npc} paints. When the last eye is done, both birds on the wall look at each other across the door, and then, very slightly, at you. {npc} climbs down and sits on the floor and laughs until {he} coughs.

choices.text: Lend {him} a feather to paint with

effects.log: A feather of your own fire for a brush. The red it lays down does not fade, and will not fade, and the archaeologists of a far later age will stand in front of it with lamps and argue about the pigment for a hundred years. (-5 health)

events.text: The last night before the tomb is sealed. {npc} has gone out to sleep under the mound. You are alone in the chamber with one lamp and the two of you on the south wall, facing each other across the dark doorway, and the paint is still wet enough to step into. A guardian on both sides of a door. For thirteen hundred years. The dead king lies in the middle of the floor, waiting for someone to stand there.

choices.text: Bless the wall and fly out before the seal

effects.log: You breathe on both birds, once each, and fly out up the passage as the masons come down it. The painting is only paint. But it is very good paint, and something of you stays in the red of it, warm, for as long as the walls stand.

choices.text: Leave a coal of yourself in the doorway, and go

effects.log: A coal of you on the threshold, between the two painted birds. It will burn low for a very long time down there in the dark. The dead king will not be cold. You will feel it, a small warmth in the north, every winter, for the rest of your life. (-8 health)

choices.text: Step into the wall, both sides at once

effects.log: You step into the wet red on the left of the door and are also, somehow, on the right, facing yourself, lotus bud in your beak, red peaks under your feet, wings raised at the instant of flight. The masons seal the tomb at dawn. In the dark you guard one door for thirteen hundred years, from both sides, and the dead king is never alone, and nothing else ever comes in.

events.text: The swallows come back on the third of the third month with a message for you from the warm country: the old king of the swallows is dying. He has heard every swallow's report of every house it nested under for longer than anyone can count, the kind houses and the cruel ones, and he would like to see the red bird once more.

choices.text: Go south at once, on the swallow road

effects.log: You fly the whole route in eleven days, the way the old song sings it, place by place, with the whole flock streaming behind. In the reed court of the warm country the old king opens one eye and says, "Ah. The warm one. Late, as usual."

choices.text: Bow to the old king as you did when you were young
