effects.log: You bow to him exactly as you did centuries ago, beak to the reed floor, and the old king laughs a thin swallow laugh. "You remembered," he says. "Nobody remembers how they bowed when they were small. I knew you would come."

choices.text: Send him a coal, carried by the fastest swallow

effects.log: A coal in a clay bead, carried south by a swallow who is very proud to be asked. The old king keeps it under his wing all winter and is warm. He sends back word: thank you, and come yourself next time.

events.text: The reed court of the swallows in the warm country. The old king is too weak to hear the reports himself now, so the swallows give them to you: this house mended a broken leg, this one knocked down a nest, this one left the eaves open in a storm so the chicks could get in. At the end, the court goes quiet and looks at you, and the old king, from his bed of feathers, says, "There. You can do it. I knew it."

choices.text: Hear every report to the end, and send seeds north to the kind houses

effects.log: It takes the whole winter. In spring a hundred swallows fly north each with a gourd seed for a kind house. In the autumn, you hear, a hundred poor families open a gourd and find rice in it, and silk, and once a carpenter with his tools.

choices.text: Say you are only a guest here

effects.log: "Everyone is only a guest," says the old king. "That is what a court is for. To decide which guests stay." He closes his eyes. The swallows look at you. Nobody has ever looked at you quite like that.

choices.text: Say the cruel houses deserve worse than goblins

effects.log: The court goes very quiet. The old king opens one eye. "Fire," he says, "is not justice. Gourds are justice. Go home and think about it." You go home and think about it, and it burns. (-2 health)

events.text: The old king of the swallows has died in the winter, and the reed throne in the warm country is empty, and the whole court has turned to the red bird who heard the reports. In the north your fires are burning, or not. Here it is always warm, and nobody needs you to be warm. They only need you to listen, and to send seeds.

choices.text: Crown the cleverest young swallow, and go home

effects.log: You crown a young swallow who once carried a coal for you and was very proud to be asked. It is a good king. Every spring after, the first swallow back under every eave in the south is, they say, a little warmer than the rest.

choices.text: Carry the seeds north yourself one last time, then decide

effects.log: You fly north with a gourd seed in your beak and drop it in the yard of the poorest kind house in the south, and look at your fires, and stay. The swallows choose a king without you. It is, they agree, what the old king expected you to do.

choices.text: Take the reed throne

effects.log: You sit down on the reed throne. It fits. Every spring after, a swallow carries a gourd seed north to a kind house in your name, and every autumn the swallows come back and tell you which houses were kind. You never see a northern summer again. You find, to your surprise, that you were made for listening.

events.text: Your Kiln on the southwest coast has a new keeper, {npc}, the last of a line of potters that has fired your fire for centuries. The other kilns along the coast have closed, burned by raiders or starved of clay. {npc} is the only one left who can make the kingfisher colour, the jade-green no one else can, and {he} cannot do it every time. One firing in five.

choices.text: Sit in the firebox through the next firing, all forty hours

effects.log: Forty hours of pine fire, and you in the heart of it, holding the heat steady when the wind turns. When {npc} opens the chamber, three pieces in five have come out kingfisher green. {He} sits down in the ash and laughs. (-8 health)

choices.text: Teach {him} to read the flame

effects.log: You perch on the stoke hole and teach {npc} the colours: the yellow that is too early, the white that is right, the blue at the edge that means the clay is drinking the smoke. {He} learns fast. Two in five, after that, without you.

choices.text: Renew the kiln fire with summer's wood

effects.log: Apricot and jujube in the firebox, rubbed new. The old fire was tired and the glaze was tired with it. The next firing comes out so green that {npc} carries the best bowl down to the shore just to see it against the sea.

events.text: A tribute vase for the court, ordered by name, and {npc} has fired it four times and lost it four times: cracked, brown, slumped, cracked. The officials come next month. {He} sits in front of the cold kiln at dusk with the fifth vase on the ground between {his} feet, raw and grey, and does not look up when you land.

choices.text: Fire it with your whole heat, and nothing else

ok.log: You go into the firebox and become it. Forty hours. When {npc} opens the chamber the vase is the green of a kingfisher's back in shade, and it rings like a bell when {he} taps it. The officials take it to the capital. Somewhere in later lives, it will still be there.

fail.log: It cracks. Fifth time. {npc} picks up the halves and puts them together and looks through the crack at you. "Again," {he} says, and you both start over. (-12 health)

choices.text: Tell {him} the court can wait a firing

effects.log: You go to the officials yourself, a red bird on the magistrate's ridge tiles, and explain that the kingfisher colour does not come when it is ordered. They wait a season, astonished. The sixth vase is perfect.

events.text: {npc} is old, and has no apprentice who can make the green, and has stopped pretending otherwise. {He} sits by the firebox of the last kingfisher kiln on the coast with {his} hand on the warm brick. "When I go," {he} says, "it goes. Unless the fire stays. You could stay. The kiln would know the colour by itself, then, for as long as anyone fired it."

choices.text: Find {him} an apprentice, and teach them both

effects.log: You find a clay-digger's child with good hands and stubborn eyes, and teach in the firebox while {npc} teaches at the wheel. It takes twenty years. One in seven, the child manages. It is enough to keep the colour in the world a little longer.

choices.text: Renew the fire one last time and promise to come back

effects.log: You rub the kiln fire new with summer's wood and promise to come back every summer, and you do, as long as {npc} lives. After that the kiln goes on without the green, firing good plain bowls, and nobody but you misses the colour.

choices.text: Lie down in the firebox and stay

effects.log: You lie down in the heart of the firebox and fold your wings. {npc} feeds the pine in, weeping. For three hundred years that kiln fires the jade-green that no one else can make, and every potter who stokes it sings to the fire without knowing why. When the last of them dies, you go out, quietly, and the secret is lost, as it was always going to be.

events.text: Your Beacon's keeper, {npc}, has been called from the coast to the capital's southern hill, where all five beacon roads end, to keep the last chimney: the one that tells the king each evening whether the country is at peace. {He} takes a coal of your fire with {him} in a clay pot, all the way up the beacon road, and sets it in the southern hill's chimney. One fire. All is well.
events.arc: One Fire on the Southern Hill

choices.text: Fly the five beacon roads to see the fire carried home

effects.log: Hill to hill, south coast to capital, every chimney lit one by one at dusk, the evening fires running north like a word passed hand to hand. At the end of all of them, on the southern hill, your coal. The king's secretary reads it and writes: peace.

choices.text: Sit on the chimney with {him} the first night

effects.log: {npc} talks all night, nervous, about the coast and the sea and the raids {he} has seen. Below you the capital goes to bed. "One fire," {he} says at dawn. "It does not look like much." "It is everything," you say, and {he} almost drops the torch.

choices.text: Renew the fire before it goes up the hill

effects.log: You rub the Beacon new with the season's wood before {npc} carries it north, so that it arrives on the southern hill young and clean. It burns, the secretaries remark, very steadily that century.

events.text: A night with no moon, and on the southern hill {npc} sees two fires come up the road from the coast instead of one, then three, then four. The capital is asleep under the hill. {He} has the torches for five in {his} hands and is shaking. It could be raiders. It could be a fool on a far hill. Five fires will wake the king.
events.arc: One Fire on the Southern Hill

choices.text: Fly down the road and read the coast yourself

ok.log: You go down the beacon road faster than the fires and see the sails yourself: real, forty of them, in the bay. You are back on the southern hill before {npc} has finished shaking, and you light five together. The capital wakes in time. That is what you are for.

fail.log: You are not sure. Smoke, rain, a far glow. You come back and cannot tell {npc} yes or no. {He} lights four and waits, and by dawn it turns out four was right. You hate not knowing. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell {him} to trust the fires and light five

effects.log: {npc} lights five. The capital wakes. The raiders are real, and the city is ready for them, and {npc} is never quite the same after: a person who has woken a king.

events.text: {npc} is dying in the hut below the southern hill's chimney, and has asked to see the fire. You carry {him} up in your claws, gently, and set {him} down by the chimney at dusk. One fire. All is well. "Who will keep it," {he} says, "when there is nobody who remembers it was yours?"
events.arc: One Fire on the Southern Hill

choices.text: Find the hill a new keeper before you leave

effects.log: A young soldier who has stood on the southern hill a year and still looks at the chimney each dusk as if it were new. You give them the coal. {npc} watches, and nods, and is content.

choices.text: Promise to come back to it every century

effects.log: You promise, and {npc} believes you, and you keep it. Every hundred years, at dusk, the keepers of the southern hill see a red bird on the chimney for one night, and none of them ever tell their officers.

choices.text: Stay. Be the one fire on the southern hill

effects.log: You settle into the chimney and are the fire. {npc} smiles and closes {his} eyes. For five hundred years, every night that nothing is wrong, the one fire on the capital's southern hill is you, and the king reads you and sleeps. The night something is, you are five.

events.text: Something turns you north one winter, and you follow it, and it is the village. It is bigger, and the road is different, and the persimmon tree is three persimmon trees later. But the house is there. The kitchen is there. And on the earthen floor the fire jar of nine generations, which is now the fire jar of many more than nine, is banked for the night with ash, and under the ash, something red.

choices.text: Look in, very quietly

effects.log: The coals under the ash are old fire, your fire, carried from mother to daughter-in-law, grandfather to grandchild, for longer than you have been a guardian. Nobody let it out. You sit on the lip of the jar all night and do not say anything to it, because it already knows.

choices.text: Renew it, very gently, so nobody notices

effects.log: You rub the old fire new in the dark with a twig of the season's wood, so carefully that in the morning the youngest of the house finds the jar exactly as it was banked, and only a little warmer.

choices.text: Remember the youngest who carried a coal of it over the pass

effects.log: A coal in a clay pot, a match over the pass, a second house warm from its first night. There are two houses with your fire in them, and their children's children's houses. You go and look at the other one too. It is also banked properly.

events.text: The coldest night of the year in the house you were born in. The keeping of the fire jar is a child's this year, and the child fell asleep, and the jar has gone cold, and in the grey ash there is nothing red at all. The child wakes in the dark and kneels by the jar and you hear a small voice say, "No. No no no."

choices.text: Drop into the jar as a single red point

effects.log: You go down into the ash as small as you were the first night, one red point that will not go out. The child digs, finds you, and blows, so softly that it is almost a question. You answer it by not going out. By dawn there is a fire. Nobody else in the house ever knows how close it came.

choices.text: Feel the old breath come down to you again

effects.log: The child blows, and lays a pine needle across you, and you eat it. Long ago, in another life, someone knelt at a jar like this and blew. You remember both sides of it now. You burn very gently, the way you were fed.

choices.text: Light the stove from outside, through the flue

effects.log: You breathe down the chimney into the cold firebox and the stove lights by itself. The child stares at it. In the morning the grandmother hears the story and says nothing, and that night talks to the fire jar the whole time she banks it, as if to a guest.

events.text: Winter again in the house you were born in, and you are sitting on the lip of the fire jar while the family sleeps. You are very large now and very old, a guardian of a quarter of the sky, and none of it is as warm as this kitchen. The jar is open. The ash is soft. It would be very easy to go back in, and stay.

choices.text: Bank the fire properly and fly back to the sky

effects.log: You bank the coals the way the youngest of the house once taught you, ash over them, lid on, and go back up to the south of the sky. Every winter after, the coldest night, you look north for one red point in one kitchen, and it is always there.

choices.text: Leave a coal of yourself in the ash and go

effects.log: A seed of you, under the ash, to keep the jar honest. You fly south. The family never knows, but nobody in that house is ever quite cold again, and once in a while, on still nights, the jar chirps. (-6 health)

choices.text: Go back into the fire jar, for good

effects.log: You go down into the ash, small, red, home. In the morning the youngest of the house lifts the lid and finds the fire burning better than it ever has. For a thousand years nobody in that line is cold, and nobody knows why the fire sometimes chirps.

events.text: A gut, a shaman's great rite, in a southern village on the first day of summer. The shaman, {npc}, dances the five directions in turn: east, the blue general; west, the white; north, the black; the centre, yellow. Then {he} opens a red fan and spins south, faster and faster, bells shaking, calling the Red Emperor of summer, and stops dead, mid-turn, facing the hill where you are sitting. The whole village turns to look where {he} is looking.

choices.text: Let {him} see you: rise over the hill at noon

effects.log: You rise over the hill in the white light and the village sees a red that is not a bird so much as the summer standing up. {npc} drops to {his} knees, and then, because {he} is a professional, gets up and finishes the dance properly. You stay till the last bell.

choices.text: Stay hidden, but warm the courtyard

effects.log: You stay behind the hill and breathe on the village, once, gently. The courtyard warms, the rice-cake steam rises straight, and {npc}, still facing you with the fan open, smiles very slightly as if to say: I know.

choices.text: Answer with one note, the way the south does

effects.log: One note, from the hill. Every bell in the courtyard rings by itself. {npc} closes the fan with a snap and bows south, and the gut goes on for three days instead of one.

events.text: {npc} has taken to divining with the five flags, folded together so the colours cannot be seen, and having the villagers draw one blind. For a whole year, whoever draws, whatever they ask, the flag is red. {He} climbs your hill in the heat with the bundle under {his} arm and sits down and asks you, quite crossly, what it means.

choices.text: "It means summer is listening"

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it, fanning {him}self with the red fan. "That is a terrible answer for a divination," {he} says. "Nobody can do anything with it." But {he} uses it, all year, and the village is unaccountably cheerful.

choices.text: Draw a flag yourself, blind

ok.log: You pull one out of the bundle with your beak. It is yellow. The centre. {npc} stares at it, and then at you, and then starts laughing so hard {he} has to lie down in the grass. "Even you," {he} says. "Even you do not know."

fail.log: Red. Of course red. {npc} looks at you with deep professional disappointment. You are a little embarrassed to be so predictable, and it sits in you, warm and itchy.

choices.text: Tell {him} to stop asking the sky what it means

effects.log: "It means what you do with it," you say. {npc} considers this. "You are a very unhelpful god," {he} says, and goes back down the hill, and does something with it.

events.text: {npc} asks a thing no shaman has asked you before. North over the mountains there is a valley where the barley never ripens, {he} says, because summer has never gone that far. {His} mother's people came from there. "You are summer," {he} says. "Not a bird. Summer. Go and be summer somewhere that has never had any."

choices.text: Go north, and sit on that valley for a whole summer

effects.log: A whole summer on a cold valley at the top of the world. The snow goes back up the slopes. The barley ripens for the first time anyone remembers. The people there have no word for you and make one up. {npc} hears about it by the next spring, and is insufferable. (-10 health)

choices.text: Send them a Hearth instead, and a keeper

effects.log: You give the valley a hearth fire, a good one, and a keeper with steady hands. It is not a summer. It is the seed of one. The barley still does not ripen, but the houses are warm, and that is where summers start. (The Hearth burns.)

choices.text: Refuse. Summer belongs where it belongs

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long time with the red fan closed. "That," {he} says, "is what the White Tiger would say." You think about that for a century. It does not get cooler.

events.text: The red fan has passed down. {npc} is the grandchild now, and dances the south the way {his} grandparent did, a little faster, a little worse, with exactly the same stop, dead, facing your hill. Afterwards {he} climbs up and sits beside you in the grass. "My grandparent said you were rude," {he} says, "and kind, and very hot, and that I should ask you what you are for."

choices.text: "For giving things away"

effects.log: "Fire," says {npc}, nodding, "is the only thing that gets bigger when you give it away." It is a good line. You suspect the grandparent wrote it. You let {him} keep it.

choices.text: "For the cold houses"

effects.log: {npc} is quiet a long time. "Mine was cold," {he} says, "when I was small. Then it was not." {He} does not ask how. {He} does not need to.

choices.text: "I am still finding out"

effects.log: "After all this time?" says {npc}, scandalised. "After all this time," you say. {He} laughs, and fans you, which is the strangest thing anyone has ever done for you.

events.text: Noon on the summer solstice, and every shaman of the south who has ever danced the red fan dances it at once, in every village, and stops dead facing you. In the sky above the four quarters four glows answer: blue, white, black, gold. The fifth seat, the red one, the seat of the Red Emperor of summer, stands open in the white noon. It is not a seat for a bird.

choices.text: Sit in it for one day, and rise again a bird

effects.log: One day. You sit, and are summer, every field and every hearth at once, and it is very large and very quiet. At sunset you get up and are a bird again, smaller, louder, and glad. The shamans of the south say it was the hottest solstice in a thousand years. They are right.

choices.text: Fly down and give the red fan back to the dancers

effects.log: You land in the nearest courtyard and bow to the shaman there, beak to the dust, and fly off. The seat stays open. The four glows wait. There is no hurry, the Yellow Dragon sends word. There never was.

choices.text: Take the red seat

effects.log: You sit, and do not get up. Every summer after this one is your breath. Every hearth in the south is a feather you dropped. On the first day of summer, in a thousand villages, a shaman spins south with a red fan, and stops dead, facing you, and you are there.

events.text: A clerk of heaven finds you on the edge of the southern sky with a scroll and an apologetic face. Heaven, it seems, keeps a provision for guardians who would like to begin again: back to the very start, a spark on the coldest night, remembering everything. It has seldom been used. "Most do not want to be small again," says the clerk. "But you were small for so short a time."

choices.text: Ask what you would remember

effects.log: "Everything," says the clerk. "Every fire, every keeper, every slope that burned. You would know, this time, from the first pine needle." You think about knowing, in a fire jar, which fires will run. It is a terrible gift. It might be the best one.

choices.text: Laugh, and send the clerk away

effects.log: The clerk goes. The scroll stays, rolled up on the edge of the sky, getting warm. You find yourself looking at it on cold nights.

choices.text: Say you would do it all the same

effects.log: "All of it?" says the clerk. "All of it," you say, and are not sure it is true. The clerk writes something on the scroll and leaves it with you, in case.

events.text: The coldest night of the year below, and you feel it from the sky: somewhere in the south a fire jar has gone cold in a house that has kept its fire for nine generations, and in the grey ash there is nothing red, and a child is kneeling there, saying no, no, no. Heaven's scroll is unrolled on the edge of the sky. It would take one step.

choices.text: Send a coal down to the jar, and stay what you are

effects.log: You drop a coal from the sky into the cold jar, so small the child takes it for a spark that held on. By dawn there is a fire. You roll the scroll up again and put it back on the edge of the sky. Not yet.

choices.text: Burn the scroll. You have one life, and this is it

effects.log: It goes up in one breath. The clerk of heaven, far off, sighs and crosses something out. Below, the child finds a red point in the ash anyway. It was not you. Fire, it turns out, is sometimes only fire, and that is enough.

choices.text: Step down into the jar, and begin again

effects.log: You step off the edge of the sky. It is a long way down and very cold, and then you are at the bottom of a clay jar in grey ash, one red point that will not go out, and a small round face comes down out of the dark, and a voice says, "No. No no no." You remember everything. This time, you think, as the pine needle comes, this time.

events.text: A clerk of heaven finds you, with a scroll and no apology, and the look of one who has done this before. The council has read your record to the end, the ash and the warmth, and it will not seat you: not this century, not the next. "You can keep the south from outside the door for as long as you like," the clerk says. "Or you can start again, knowing."

choices.text: Keep the south from outside the door

effects.log: You stay. Outside the council door, unseated, you keep the south the way you always have: you fly the circuit, you renew what is old, you sit on ridge-poles in the rain. Nobody in the south knows the seat was ever shut. The clerk leaves the scroll on the step.

choices.text: Ask to see the ash, county by county

effects.log: The clerk unrolls a map of the south with the ash on it in grey, every slope and roof and banquet hat. It is less than you feared and more than you remembered. You look at it until you can name every grey place. The clerk waits, and then goes.

choices.text: Step down into the jar, and begin again

effects.log: You take the scroll and step off the edge of the sky. It is a long way down and very cold, and then you are a red point in the grey ash of a clay jar, and a small round face comes down out of the dark. You remember everything: every slope, every hat. This time, you think, as the pine needle comes, less ash.

events.text: You go north in a column of heat to the ridge where the five-coloured bird lives, the one the kings like, the one every painter confuses with you, and land on the ridge opposite. Every paulownia between you curls its leaves. "The south wall of the sky is too big for one bird," you sing across. "Share it with me. Fire and wood. They would paint us together." The Phoenix looks at you a long time and says: "I hold nothing. I only come."

choices.text: "That is the most frightening thing I have ever heard a bird say"

effects.log: You mean it. A guardian holds a wall; a fire holds a house; you have never in your life held nothing. You do not leave. You sit on the opposite ridge until dark, looking at a bird who can simply come, and go.

choices.text: Tell it the truth: you came for company

effects.log: "The guardians hold their walls alone," you say. "Every summer I burn, and every summer nobody burns with me." Then, quickly: "Not that I mind." The Phoenix says nothing. It does not leave either.

choices.text: Laugh, and set three of its trees smouldering

effects.log: You laugh, a shower of sparks, and three paulownias on its slope begin to smoke. "I came to share," you say, "not to be given. You do not understand fire at all." It is a good line. The trees are still smouldering when you leave. (Ash +1)

events.text: You go back north, and this time you bring the south with you: a summer that will not end, the paulownias on the five-coloured bird's slope browning at the edges in the ninth month. "Then fight me for it," you sing. "If you will not share the south, take it. Guardians are made that way." The Phoenix does not strike. It begins, very quietly, to sing five notes.

choices.text: Listen to the five notes to the end

effects.log: Wood answers fire with music, not more fire. Your flames go low and blue as you listen. At the end you hear yourself say, "Cousin," which you have never said to anyone, and go home south with the summer folded under your wing.

choices.text: Follow it north singing insults, then stop

effects.log: It rises and flies north out of the heat without looking back, and you follow it a hundred li, singing every insult you know, and then you stop in the middle of the sky, and the summer ends that night all at once, like a door closing. You do not know why you stopped. You do know.

choices.text: Burn its slope anyway

effects.log: You burn a whole slope of its trees while it sings. It does not stop singing. It sings over the fire until the fire is ashamed of itself, and so are you. (Ash +1)

events.text: A last visit, in the dead of winter, when you are small and almost cool. You land on the Phoenix's own branch, which you have never done. "They paint us together," you say. "Every painter in the south. Every banner. Red bird, five-coloured bird, nobody can tell which is which. I used to mind. Do you?"

choices.text: Lean against it, very slightly, and singe nothing

effects.log: "No," it says, "let them paint us together," and you lean against it very slightly, which singes nothing at all, which is the hardest thing you have done all century. From then on the southern painters, without knowing why, leave a little space between the two birds.

choices.text: Ask it for one feather, and hold it without burning it

effects.log: One five-coloured feather. You hold it a long time without burning it, which costs you something. You are never seen in the south again without it. When the painters do get you wrong, now, they are at least a little right. (-6 health)

choices.text: Say: "Then they can be wrong about both of us"

effects.log: It laughs, a low wooden sound. You part as cousins, which is what you were, and fly south through the snow carrying more warmth than you came with, which for fire is not usual.

events.text: The Southern Palace is yours now, and it is seven halls in a line, and every one of them is cold. The Hall of the Well with its lamp for the law; the Hall of the Ghost with its candles for the dead; the Willow, the Seven Stars, the Net, the Wings, the Chariot. Nobody has lit them since the last bird who sat in the south, if there was one. You walk the courtyard with a live coal in your beak, and it must not go out.

choices.text: Light them in order, Well to Chariot, one each day

effects.log: Seven days. On the first, the Well's lamp, and the law in the world below reads a little clearer. On the last, the Chariot's, and the wind turns kind. The palace is warm by the end of the week, and so, strangely, are you.

choices.text: Light the Net first, the kitchen, so guests can be fed

effects.log: A palace is only a palace when the kitchen is lit. You light the great stove of the Extended Net first, and the smell of rice goes out along the clouds, and by evening there are guests. The south is the south again.

choices.text: Run from hall to hall lighting all seven at once

ok.log: Seven halls in one noon, the coal never out of your beak. The palace goes up warm all at once like a house waking. The clouds round it steam for a week.

fail.log: You run too fast and the coal drops on the steps of the Wings. One step catches; it is a stone step; it should not be able to. You put it out. The scorch stays. (Ash +1, -8 health)

events.text: In the Hall of the Net, the kitchen of heaven that keeps the guests fed, a long table is laid for the summer solstice banquet. When you come to count the places there is one more seat than guests, and its cushion is scorched. Nobody laid it. It was there when you lit the hall. The kitchen spirits say it has always been there: the seat of the guest who burned.

choices.text: Leave it empty, and set a cup at it every year

effects.log: Every solstice a full cup at the scorched seat, and nobody sits there. It becomes the custom of the south. Long after, guests from the world below will raise their cups to it before they sit, and you will bow to them for it.

choices.text: Ask the kitchen spirits who it was

effects.log: "Somebody who came too close to the fire for warmth," says the oldest spirit. "Every fire has one. Yours too." You think of a keeper who died in a fire you forgot to renew, and you do not ask again.

choices.text: Let any brave guest sit there, if they dare

effects.log: The seat is hot as a stove lid and leaves a red print. Very few dare. Those who do, you decide, are either rude or brave, and in the south that is often the same thing.

events.text: The Hall of the Wings governs distant visitors, and this year they come: travellers from the far quarters of heaven, a frost-spirit from the north edge with icicles in its sleeves, a wind-clerk from the west, a river god from the east who drips on the floor. They arrive cold and tired and suspicious of the south.

choices.text: Bow to each guest first, at the gate

effects.log: You bow at the gate of the Wings to every guest, first and low, the way you were made to bow at the council when you were the youngest. The frost-spirit is so surprised it melts a little. Courtesy, you have learned, is how fire says welcome without burning anyone.

choices.text: Seat them by the fire, the cold ones nearest

effects.log: The frost-spirit sits furthest from the fire and slowly, over the evening, moves its cushion closer. By midnight it is telling stories. The river god dries out and is much better company.

choices.text: Keep them waiting at the gate. The south is busy

effects.log: You are busy, and you are proud, and you keep them waiting. They go home cold and tell the far quarters about the south. You wanted to be the youngest who learned manners. You find you have to learn them again. (-2 health)

events.text: The Hall of the Seven Stars, the neck of the bird, governs urgent matters, and a bell in it rings by itself one night: somewhere on earth a beacon is burning five and nobody is answering it. A coast, a raid, a capital asleep. From up here it is a red point the size of a grain of millet. Down there it is everything.

choices.text: Go down, now, as fast as the neck of the bird can carry you

effects.log: You go down out of the sky like a thrown coal and wake the next beacon, and the next, and the capital, and the coast is ready by dawn. You come back up to the palace with your feathers singed and the bell silent. Urgent matters are what you are for. (-10 health)

choices.text: Send a wind down the beacon road from the Chariot

effects.log: You send the Chariot's wind down the beacon road and it blows the five fires bright and tall all the way north, hill to hill, until somebody in the capital wakes and looks. It is slower than going yourself. It works.

choices.text: Ring the bell back. Earth must learn to answer itself

effects.log: You ring back, and wait. Somebody answers, late. The coast is half ready. A village burns that need not have. It is the right lesson for earth and the wrong night to teach it, and you know it.

events.text: One noon you notice that you are no longer a bird who guards summer. You are summer. The heat on the paddies is you; the smoke going up straight from every hearth on a still evening is you; the bird is a shape you put on, now, when you want to talk to someone. The shamans of the south have started calling you the Red Emperor. You did not ask them to.

choices.text: Put the bird shape on and sit on a ridge-pole, to remember

effects.log: You sit on the ridge of a farmhouse at dusk, a red bird, and a child below throws a pebble at you, and misses, and you are so pleased to be small enough to be missed that you stay till dark.

choices.text: Spread out into the whole south, and listen

effects.log: Every kitchen, every kiln, every ferry lantern, every candle on every altar shelf. You hear them all at once, a low warm roar like a city of fires talking. Somewhere in it is the fire jar of the house you were born in. You can pick it out, still.

choices.text: Ask the Yellow Dragon what an emperor of a season is for

effects.log: "For ending on time," says the Yellow Dragon, which is the least comforting answer you could have had. Then, more kindly: "And for beginning again next year. That is the whole of it. You will be good at the second part."

events.text: The end of summer, and the White Tiger is waiting on the western ridge with autumn behind it, the way it does every year. It does not ask any more. It waits. You have learned, over the centuries, that letting go of summer on time is the one thing the Red Emperor must do perfectly, every year, for ever.

choices.text: Give autumn over with a bow, on the right day

effects.log: You bow toward the west and fold the summer in. The Tiger bows back across the whole width of the land. The persimmons redden that week. It is a small rite. You have never once been late for it since you learned how.

choices.text: Give it over a day early, as a gift

effects.log: A day early. The Tiger notices; of course it notices. The next spring there is a white feather on your ridge, stiff with frost, which is a tiger's idea of thanks. You keep it in the Net with the rest.

choices.text: Hold it one more day, for the late rice

effects.log: One more day, for a valley where the rice was planted late. The Tiger waits. It is only a day. You know exactly how days add up.

events.text: A child in a southern village asks a grandmother why summer comes, and the grandmother, who has kept the fire jar of her house for sixty years, says: "Because a red bird brings it, every year, and it has never once forgotten." You are on the ridge-pole above them in the bird shape, listening.

choices.text: Let a feather fall into the yard

effects.log: One red feather, still warm, lands in the dust at the child's feet. The grandmother looks up, too late to see anything. The child keeps the feather in a box for years and gives it to a grandchild with the same explanation.

choices.text: Correct her, gently: it has forgotten, sometimes

effects.log: You say it from the ridge-pole, quietly. The grandmother is not at all surprised to be answered by a roof. "Yes," she says. "But it came back." The child looks from one of you to the other and decides that is a better story.

events.text: A feather of the Seven Stars itches, then burns, and you look down and see why: the Hearth you gave has sixty years on it and nobody rubbed it new. Tonight it is out of the fire jar and across the kitchen floor and into the paper door, and the house next to it is thatch.

choices.text: Come down out of the sky with summer's wood and rub it new

ok.log: You come down like a thrown coal with apricot and jujube in your claws and rub sixty years of fire young in one breath. The Hearth settles, and the star in you settles with it. Nobody is hurt. (-10 health)

fail.log: Too old to renew. You fight it until dawn and lose, and the Hearth you gave is gone, and a dark place opens in your feathers where its star was. The ash is yours. (Ash +5, -15 health)

choices.text: Call it home into your breast

effects.log: You draw the whole fire up into yourself, sixty years of it, burning. The Hearth is lost, and its star goes dark in your plumage. Nothing else burns. (-8 health)

choices.text: Let it run. A star can spare one fire

effects.log: You stay in the sky and watch it run. The Hearth goes over the ridge and on, and the star that was it smears and goes out, and the swallows will not nest in that county for a generation. (Ash +5)

events.text: The Ghost, before your head, has a red smear across it tonight. Your Rite Candle, sixty years unrenewed, has leapt into the banners of a lineage hall at the midnight rite, and the hall is old dry wood full of people bowing.

choices.text: Come down out of the sky with summer's wood and rub it new

ok.log: You come down like a thrown coal with apricot and jujube in your claws and rub sixty years of fire young in one breath. The Rite Candle settles, and the star in you settles with it. Nobody is hurt. (-10 health)

fail.log: Too old to renew. You fight it until dawn and lose, and the Rite Candle you gave is gone, and a dark place opens in your feathers where its star was. The ash is yours. (Ash +5, -15 health)

choices.text: Call it home into your breast

effects.log: You draw the whole fire up into yourself, sixty years of it, burning. The Rite Candle is lost, and its star goes dark in your plumage. Nothing else burns. (-8 health)

choices.text: Let it run. A star can spare one fire

effects.log: You stay in the sky and watch it run. The Rite Candle goes over the ridge and on, and the star that was it smears and goes out, and the swallows will not nest in that county for a generation. (Ash +5)

events.text: Beside the Well, the Axe has turned to look at a star in your neck. On earth the Lamp of the Court, sixty years on its desk, has jumped to the shelves of the county records office, and the registers of a whole county are catching.

choices.text: Come down out of the sky with summer's wood and rub it new

ok.log: You come down like a thrown coal with apricot and jujube in your claws and rub sixty years of fire young in one breath. The Lamp of the Court settles, and the star in you settles with it. Nobody is hurt. (-10 health)

fail.log: Too old to renew. You fight it until dawn and lose, and the Lamp of the Court you gave is gone, and a dark place opens in your feathers where its star was. The ash is yours. (Ash +5, -15 health)

effects.log: You draw the whole fire up into yourself, sixty years of it, burning. The Lamp of the Court is lost, and its star goes dark in your plumage. Nothing else burns. (-8 health)

effects.log: You stay in the sky and watch it run. The Lamp of the Court goes over the ridge and on, and the star that was it smears and goes out, and the swallows will not nest in that county for a generation. (Ash +5)

events.text: A court geomancer, very senior, very tired, has climbed to the ridge where you sit with a compass board strapped to {his} back. {npc} has a letter from the palace, as the geomancers always do. This one is different. It does not ask you to leave the fire mountain. It asks where, if you were a capital, you would want to be built.

choices.text: "Facing south, on a river, with a hill in front to dance on"

effects.log: {npc} writes it all down in a careful hand: the river, the hill, the dancing. "The dancing?" {he} asks. "Every capital needs one hill that is not afraid of fire," you say. {He} underlines it twice.

choices.text: "Somewhere with good kitchens. The rest follows"

mem.note: said build where the kitchens are good

effects.log: {npc} laughs for the first time in the conversation. Then {he} thinks about it and stops laughing, and goes down the mountain looking at every village chimney on the way.

choices.text: "Ask the Yellow Dragon. The middle is its business"

effects.log: {npc} sighs. "I did," {he} says. "It pretended to be asleep." You are not surprised. You give {him} a little warmth for the climb down anyway.

events.text: A grandmaster who has beaten everyone under heaven worth beating stands in the yard below your ridge in a plain grey robe. {npc} does not bow. "They say the Summer Bird has never lost a fight it cared about," {he} says. "I would like to be the one it cared about."

choices.text: Come down and give {him} the fight

mem.note: beat me fairly when I fought you

ok.log: It lasts from noon to the hour of the dog. The yard is glass in places. At the end {npc} is on one knee and laughing, and you are on the ridge again, smoking slightly. "You cared," {he} says. "I felt it." {He} is right.

mem.note: let me put a cut on your wing

fail.log: A cut across your wing, clean and cold, the first in a century. {npc} lowers the sword and looks at the red on it, and bows at last, very deeply. (-18 health)

choices.text: "I care about kitchens. Go and fight a cold one"

mem.note: told me to fight a cold kitchen

effects.log: {npc} stands in the yard a long time. Then {he} goes and finds a cold kitchen in the village below and spends a winter learning to keep a fire in it, which is, {he} writes later, the hardest opponent of {his} life.

events.text: A human has climbed to your ridge who is, as far as you can tell, as old and as strong as you: {npc}, a cultivator of the highest realm under heaven, sitting cross-legged on the tiles a polite distance from the heat. "Everyone I know is either afraid of me or dead," {he} says. "You are neither. Would you like to be friends?"

choices.text: "Yes. Come and sit closer, if you can bear it"

effects.log: {npc} moves a little closer, then a little more, until {his} sleeve is smoking, and stays there. You talk until dawn about nothing: weather, kitchens, the failings of the Jade court. It is the best night you have had in an age.

choices.text: "Friends with fire? Ask the moths how that goes"

effects.log: "I am not a moth," says {npc}. "I know," you say. "That is why I warned you." {He} comes back the next year anyway, and the year after. In the end you stop warning.

events.text: An envoy of the Jade court with a ledger under {his} arm has come to the ridge in person, which envoys never do. {npc} is auditing the Four Guardians one by one, quietly, before the great audit. "The tortoise gave me its shell," {he} says. "The tiger gave me a deer. What will the south give me?"

choices.text: "A song. Sit down; it is long"

mem.note: sang me your whole record from a roof

effects.log: {npc} sits on the courtyard steps and listens to the whole south, fire by fire, until the stars come out. At the end {he} closes the ledger without writing anything in it. "I will remember it differently from you," {he} says. "That is the idea," you say.

choices.text: "The ugly verses first, then the warm ones"

mem.note: began your confession with your ash

effects.log: You sing every slope that burned before you sing a single warm kitchen. {npc} stops writing halfway and looks up at you on the ridge. "Nobody begins with the ash," {he} says. "Somebody should," you say.

choices.text: "A hot seat. Sit on my ridge and see how long you last"

effects.log: {npc} climbs up, sits, and lasts nearly an hour, and comes down with the ledger smoking and a print on {his} robe that will never wash out. {He} writes, in red: the south is exactly as reported. (Ash +1)

events.text: An immortal of the high heavens stands under your ridge in a robe of pale gold and looks up at you with an expression you have not seen in centuries: a child's, kneeling at a fire jar. "I was the youngest of a cold house once," says {npc}. "In some life. I do not remember which. I only remember blowing on something red."

choices.text: "I remember. You blew too hard, the first time"

mem.note: remembered me blowing on the fire jar

effects.log: {npc} laughs and cries at once, which immortals are not supposed to do. You come down off the ridge and sit beside {him} on the step, small and red, and let {him} warm {his} hands on you as if on a fire jar.

choices.text: "Everyone was the youngest of a cold house, once"

mem.note: said everyone was the youngest once

effects.log: {npc} thinks about that for a long time. "Then you must have been very busy," {he} says at last. You admit it.

events.text: A sovereign of the immortal courts arrives under your ridge with a retinue of forty and a proposal, delivered beautifully. {npc} would like the south: its summers, its kitchens, its bird. In return the south would have a court, a title, a hall of red lacquer in a palace with nine gates, and an excellent salary of incense.

choices.text: "The south is not a province. It is a direction"

mem.note: told me the south is a direction

effects.log: {npc} opens {his} mouth, closes it, and looks at the retinue, none of whom can help. "One cannot own a direction," {he} says slowly. "No," you agree. "Only face it." The retinue goes home facing north.

choices.text: Bow first, very low, and say nothing at all

effects.log: You bow, beak to the tiles, and stay down. {npc} waits for the answer. It does not come. After an hour {he} understands that it has, and bows back, and leaves, and is oddly respectful of the south for the rest of a very long reign.

choices.text: Swallow it, and decline politely

effects.log: You decline in the most courteous language the south has. Under it is a word you do not say, and it goes down hot. {npc} bows and goes. (-2 health)

choices.text: Let the anger out at the word salary

effects.log: The word does it. The retinue's banners go up first, all forty, and then the canopy over {npc}, who stands perfectly still inside the fire and lets it burn out round {him}. "Noted," says the sovereign. (Ash +1)

events.text: An old astronomer from the capital has climbed the highest hill in the south with a brass sighting tube to look at you, the stars of you, and finds the actual bird sitting on the observatory roof. {npc} is not frightened. {He} is annoyed. "Your Wings," {he} says, "have been out of place by a finger's width for three years. Is it deliberate?"

choices.text: "I was leaning toward a cold house"

mem.note: told me why the Wings lean

effects.log: {npc} writes in the margin of {his} star tables: the Wings lean toward the cold. The next astronomer to read it thinks it is poetry. It is not.

choices.text: Straighten them, right now, while {he} watches

mem.note: let me watch you straighten your stars

effects.log: You shift, a little, and twenty-two stars slide a finger's width across the sky. {npc} looks through the tube and then at you and then sits down on the observatory floor. "Thank you," {he} says faintly. "That has been bothering me."

events.text: A lantern-bearer's descendant, many generations on, with the same steady hands and the same habit of holding a lamp a little too high. {npc} has inherited a story with the lantern, about a red bird and somebody who loved it and grew old. "Was it true?" {he} asks. "The family argues about it at every rite."

choices.text: "It was true. Hold the lamp lower; your ancestor never would"

mem.note: said the family story was true

effects.log: {npc} lowers the lamp, and then raises it again, exactly as high as before, and you laugh until a roof tile cracks. Some things are inherited whole.

choices.text: "Tell me your family's version first"

effects.log: It is mostly wrong, and much better than what happened. You correct nothing. {npc} goes home and tells it at the next rite exactly as before, with one new line: the bird liked this version.

events.text: One of the stars in your feathers has grown hot and too bright, and you know what it means below: an old fire of yours, thirty years or more unrenewed, and fevers in the houses round it, and quarrels at supper over nothing.

choices.text: Go down to the Hearth with summer's wood

effects.log: Apricot and jujube, rubbed new in the old fire jar before dawn. The fevers break in a week, and the star in your Seven Stars cools to its proper red.

choices.text: Go down to the Field Fire and burn the slope new

effects.log: You burn the old fire out of the slope and start it again from new wood, carefully, against the wind. The fire-field village sleeps through the night for the first time in a year.

choices.text: Go down to the Lantern and renew it on its pole

effects.log: You rub the ferry lantern new at midnight. The ferry hands stop quarrelling, and a cough that has gone up and down that river all winter goes away.

choices.text: Dim the star from above, and leave the fire for now

effects.log: You fold the hot star into your feathers and hold it low. The fevers ease a little. The fire is still old. It will not wait for you to be less busy.

events.text: A star near your crop flares white: on the coast and in the kiln country an old fire of yours has grown fierce. Pots crack in the firing for no reason; the beacon soldiers see sails in the fog and fight about it.

choices.text: Renew the Kiln with summer's wood

effects.log: Into the firebox with an armful of new wood. The next firing comes out whole, every piece, and the potters stop shouting at the apprentices.

choices.text: Renew the Beacon on its chimney

effects.log: You rub the beacon fire new at dusk. The soldiers see one fire and the sea and nothing else, and sleep in turns again.

choices.text: Leave it a season. The sky is busy

effects.log: You leave it. The star stays white. Next spring the swallows report worse, as they always do.

events.text: The Ghost before your head is restless, and the Axe beside the Well is looking hard at your neck: the Rite Candle or the Lamp of the Court has grown fierce. At the rites the dead will not settle; in the office the clerks see guilt in every face.

choices.text: Renew the Rite Candle at the midnight rite

effects.log: In with the incense smoke, new wood rubbed to new flame on the altar shelf. The ancestors settle like birds on a roof at dusk, and the Ghost goes quiet in the sky.

choices.text: Renew the Lamp of the Court on its desk

effects.log: At midnight on the clerk's desk, new wood rubbed to new flame. In the morning an honest witness is let go, and the Axe turns back to its Well.

choices.text: Sing to it from the sky, to calm it for now

effects.log: A song from the south of the sky. It helps, the way a song does. It is not new wood.

events.text: Three of your stars are white at once, and the south under them is full of fevers and quarrels. The other guardians have noticed: a note comes from the north in a cold hand, one word long. It says: Well?

choices.text: Fly the whole circuit without resting, renewing as you go

ok.log: One season, every fire in the south rubbed new, one after another. Your stars cool one by one to red. You send the north one word back: Done. (-12 health)

fail.log: Two fires renewed, and then you fall out of the sky into a paddy and lie there a week. The third star stays white. (-18 health)

choices.text: Ask the swallows where the youngest children are, and go there first

effects.log: The swallows tell you. You go there first, then the second, and the third is a little worse for waiting. That is what choosing is.

choices.text: Write back to the north: "Busy"

effects.log: You write it and send it and know exactly how it reads. The serpent will enjoy it. The fevers go on below while you are being clever. (-2 health)

events.text: A star in your feathers has gone dim and blinking, the way a fire does when nobody feeds it. A keeper of yours has died, and nobody in the house has taken the fire on.

choices.text: The Hearth: the neighbour's child who always came to warm up

effects.log: The neighbour's child has been sneaking in to warm up at that hearth for years. You make the jar blink at the child until the child carries it home under a coat. The star steadies.

choices.text: The Field Fire: a family new to the slope

effects.log: A family burned out of somewhere else has come to the slope with nothing. You show the eldest daughter where the old fire is banked under a stone. By autumn there is millet.

choices.text: The Lantern: the ferry's new hand, who is afraid of the dark

effects.log: The new ferry hand has been poling in the dark and praying. One night the lantern on the pole lights itself. The hand bows to it, and never misses a night of keeping it.

choices.text: Let the house decide. A fire nobody wants goes out gently

effects.log: You do nothing. It was theirs to decide. Perhaps someone will take it on; perhaps it will go out in the spring, with no harm in it.

events.text: The swallows bring it, and the star confirms it: a keeper is dead on the coast or in the kiln country or at a lineage hall, no heir, and the fire is guttering where nobody tends it.

choices.text: The Kiln: the old potter's sullen apprentice

effects.log: You sit in the cold firebox and wait. The apprentice comes in the night, as you knew the apprentice would. The kingfisher colour stays in the world a little longer.

choices.text: The Beacon: a widow who climbs the hill at dusk anyway

effects.log: She has climbed the hill every dusk since the burial to light the one fire, unpaid. You see that it lights every time. The army, in the end, puts her on the roll.

choices.text: The Rite Candle: the lineage's youngest, bored at the rites

effects.log: You flicker at the bored child during the rite until the child looks, and is caught. Decades later the same child, very old, is still lighting it and telling the young ones to watch.

choices.text: Let it go. Someone else's fire will warm that place

effects.log: You let it gutter. It goes out in the spring with no harm in it. You will light another somewhere else.

events.text: The clerk who kept your Lamp of the Court has died at the desk, and the new one keeps your fire in a cupboard. The star by the Axe has gone dim, and the Axe is watching the county.

choices.text: Find it a keeper: the junior copyist who stays after dark

effects.log: The junior copyist stays late every night finishing other people's work. You let the cupboard door swing open. The copyist reads by your lamp for years, and every forged deed in the county blackens in its light.

choices.text: Leave it in the cupboard. Courts get the light they deserve

effects.log: It goes out among the files that winter, without harm. The county reads its deeds by cheap oil for a generation, and a great many of them are forged.

events.text: A banquet in a palace of the high heavens, and you on the eaves because the lanterns are yours. A minor immortal, a little drunk on peach wine, remarks to the table that the southern guardian is a sort of large festive chicken. The table laughs. Your crest stands up.

choices.text: Swallow it

effects.log: You hold your crest down as if with a fist. The table laughs on. It is not much of a joke. It goes down very hot. (-2 health)

choices.text: Sing it: a verse about a chicken at a banquet of immortals

effects.log: A verse to a drinking tune, about a chicken who came to heaven and found the immortals duller than the farmyard. The table laughs harder, at the immortal now, who laughs too, eventually.

choices.text: Let it out

effects.log: Your crest goes up a yard and every lantern on the pavilion flares, and two catch, and the immortal's fan, and the edge of a cloud. Nobody is hurt. The table is very quiet. (Ash +1)

choices.text: It will not go down: try to swallow it anyway

effects.log: You try. It comes up anyway, too much has gone down before it: the eaves under you smoke, and the immortal's hat, and you have swallowed and let out at once, the worst of both. (Ash +1, -3 health)

events.text: A drought county far below holds a rite for rain in its market square, and the magistrate reads out a charge against the red stars of the south: that they are a fever in the sky, that the bird who is them is a thief of rain. A drum, a paper bird on a pole, a great many people listening.

choices.text: Swallow it

effects.log: You stay in the sky and take every word. A fever. A thief. You keep all of it, and it is a great deal to keep. (-2 health)

choices.text: Ask the Azure Dragon, very politely, for one rain

effects.log: You fly east and bow on its ridge, fire to water, which costs more than any temper. The rain comes to that county a week later. The magistrate takes the credit. You let him.

choices.text: Let it out

effects.log: The paper bird on the pole goes up first, then the pole, then the awning over the drum. The magistrate runs. The county watches its rain rite burn in a drought. (Ash +2)

choices.text: It will not go down: try to swallow it anyway

effects.log: It will not go down. It comes out of you in one hot breath across the square, and the drum skin splits, and you are still full of it after. (Ash +2, -4 health)

events.text: A young guardian of some lesser quarter, a river spirit promoted last century, passes you on the clouds and does not bow. Then, a little further on, it says to its companion, quite loudly, that the south has got above itself since it was seated.

choices.text: Swallow it

effects.log: You let it go by. Somewhere inside, the remark joins the others, in the warm dark place where you keep them. (-2 health)

choices.text: Bow to it first, as the north once made you

effects.log: You turn and bow to it, first and low, the way the youngest bows. It stops dead. Then it bows back so far it nearly falls off the cloud, and is, ever after, the most courteous spirit in heaven.

choices.text: Let it out

effects.log: You flare, once. The river spirit's sleeve steams and it yelps and runs for its river. The companion bows to you very deeply on the way past. (Ash +1)

choices.text: It will not go down: try to swallow it anyway

effects.log: You try to let it pass. It does not pass: a cloud behind you goes up in a sheet of red, and rains ash on a county below for an afternoon. (Ash +1, -3 health)

events.text: At the council, the Black Tortoise's serpent, reading a plate of your record, adds an aside of its own, dry as river ice: "And here the south laughed at something. Again." The tortoise does not stop it. The Tiger looks at its paws.

choices.text: Swallow it, for the council's dignity

effects.log: You sit very still. The serpent watches you not laughing with real interest, and moves on. It goes down slowly, like a hot stone. (-2 health)

choices.text: Sing the aside back to the serpent, in its own voice

effects.log: You sing it back, dry, a little flat, exactly like the serpent. The Tiger makes a noise like a rockfall. The tortoise writes: the south replied. The serpent, after a long moment, almost smiles.

choices.text: Laugh. Again

effects.log: You laugh. The plate smokes at the corner. The serpent, who expected nothing else, puts it out with its tail and writes: again. (Ash +1)

choices.text: It will not go down: try to swallow it anyway

effects.log: You try to hold it and the plate in the serpent's coils catches on its own, from across the terrace, from your look alone. The council adjourns. (Ash +1, -3 health)

events.text: Noon on the summer solstice, and the day is yours to hold or to let turn. The barley wants one more hot week; the wells want rain; the west is waiting, very patiently, on its ridge.

choices.text: Let the day turn on time

effects.log: You open your wings at the right moment and the longest day begins, very slightly, to shorten. Nobody below notices. That is what doing it right looks like.

choices.text: Hold it a few days longer, for the barley

effects.log: A few more days of long gold noon. The barley fills. The wells drop a hand-span. In the west the White Tiger does not move, but you know it has counted.

choices.text: Cross the sun at noon, as the truce allows, and sing

effects.log: You cross the sun at noon and every rooster in the south crows at the red hour. Inside the sun the three-legged crow pretends it is a courtesy. The day turns on time.

events.text: The dog days, the three hottest stretches after the solstice, when the old books say metal hides from fire. The White Tiger is in its cave on the western ridge with its eyes shut, waiting them out, and you are on a rock outside the cave mouth with the whole of summer behind you.

choices.text: Sit outside and talk about the weather, as you always do

effects.log: For hours. Rain, wells, a hailstorm two centuries ago that you both still think about. The Tiger answers from the dark in single words. By the end of the dog days it has said nearly forty. A record.

choices.text: Bring it ice from a mountain spring, carried in your beak

effects.log: Ice, carried by fire, which is a miracle of a small, stupid kind. Most of it melts. The Tiger licks the rest off the rock and looks at you as if you were entirely mad, and is grateful. (-4 health)

choices.text: Stretch the dog days a little, for the fun of it

effects.log: You lean on the heat for a week past its time. Inside the cave the Tiger opens one eye. It does not say anything. It does not need to.

events.text: The Beacon star at the tip of your tail flickers two, three, four. On the southern coast raiders out of the islands across the strait have come again, the way they have come for centuries: a fleet in the bay at dusk, the fishing villages emptying, one beacon post after another lighting more fires.

choices.text: Come down on the fleet

ok.log: You come down out of the night like the whole south falling. The sails go first. The fleet turns for the strait with half its ships burning on the water, and the villages come back down from the hills at dawn.

fail.log: They have learned about you: wet hides over the decks, archers with fire-arrows of their own. You turn them, barely, and limp back to the beacon hill with arrows in your tail feathers. (-16 health)

choices.text: Light every beacon up the coast so the capital wakes in time

effects.log: Hill to hill, five fires, north faster than any rider. The garrisons are on the beaches by morning. Nobody sees you do it; it is only the beacons, doing what beacons do, unusually well.

choices.text: Burn the raiders' landing and the shore with it

effects.log: The beach goes up and the boats on it, and the fishing huts above the tide line. The raiders do not land. The village comes back to ashes. (Ash +1)

events.text: A raid long over, on a stretch of coast you could not cover: a village picking through what is left, the boats burnt, the granary empty, the old people sitting on the sea wall saying nothing. Their cooking fires are out. Nobody has had the heart to light them again.

choices.text: Go down and light every cooking fire in the village

effects.log: One by one, every kitchen. The smell of rice gets up off the shore by evening and the old people on the sea wall turn round. That is how a village decides to stay. (-4 health)

choices.text: Warm the sea wall where the old people sit

effects.log: The stones under them go warm as a heated floor. Nobody moves for a long time. Then somebody starts to talk, about the next boats, and the nets, and who has seed rice left.

events.text: There is a market in the hills now that sells nothing but you: red feathers, real and dyed, cinnabar ground with your name on the jar, nets of chain rented by the day. The traders look up whenever the evening goes red, and reach under the table.

choices.text: Go quiet, and fly only at night for a while

effects.log: You fly by night and sleep in chimneys for a season. The market sells dyed chicken feathers to the gullible and grumbles. It does not close.

choices.text: Drop one real feather on the stall, freely given, and go

effects.log: A real one, still warm, on the counter. The trader stares at it, then up at you, then puts it in a box and does not sell it, ever. The market is less sure of itself after that.

choices.text: Burn the nets under the tables

effects.log: The chain does not burn; the ropes and the stalls do. The traders scatter. They are back in a month with better nets. (Ash +1)

events.text: Hunters on your trail again: a dozen with soaked chain nets and a cart, following the smoke of your fires from kiln to beacon to ferry, asking every keeper where you sleep.

choices.text: Lead them in a circle for a month, through the wettest country

ok.log: Marsh after marsh, rain after rain. At the end of the month the hunters are sitting in a paddy with their nets full of frogs. They go home.

fail.log: They are better than you thought. A net catches your tail at a river crossing and you tear free with feathers left behind, which they sell. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let the keepers tell them nothing, and fly north a while

effects.log: Every keeper they ask looks blank. A potter, a ferry hand, a beacon soldier, a grandmother at a fire jar: nobody has ever heard of a red bird. You are prouder of that than of anything you did that year.

events.text: Buddha's birthday in a county of the southeast, and the people have hung their falling fire over the pond below the pavilion: sticks of oak charcoal wrapped in paper, thousands on long cords, lit one by one until fire drips into the water like petals. Lotus lanterns on the water. Everyone looking up. Some of them are looking at you.

choices.text: Breathe along the cords so every one catches at once

effects.log: The whole pond flowers at once, a curtain of falling fire from bank to bank, and the crowd makes a single sound. The old people say they have never seen it fall so evenly. They are right.

choices.text: Keep every spark on the water and off the roofs

effects.log: A wind comes up off the hill halfway through and you lean on every spark that tries to drift toward the thatch. Not one lands anywhere but the pond. Nobody knows. That is fine.

choices.text: Laugh with the crowd

effects.log: You laugh at the children chasing sparks along the bank, and the laugh is hotter than you meant: the pavilion's awning catches. They put it out with pond water and cheer, as if it were part of the show. (Ash +1)

events.text: The lantern festival in the capital, the old one, ten thousand lamps along the streets and up the temple steps, and in every one of them a flame that, if you look closely, leans a little toward the south.

choices.text: Walk the streets in a small shape, a red sparrow among the lamps

effects.log: Nobody looks twice at a red sparrow at a lantern festival. You sit on a lamp-post and listen to a family argue about dumplings, and a child gives you a crumb, and it is the best night of the century.

choices.text: Brighten every lamp at midnight, once

effects.log: At midnight every lamp in the capital flares at once, and the whole city looks up, and you are already a red streak going home.

events.text: The swallows are back on the third of the third month, and one of them will not settle on its eave. It has news from a house it nested under: a keeper of yours has turned the fire to harm.

choices.text: Hear it out: A hearth fire of yours is being used to burn a neighbour's barn over a boundary stone

effects.log: The swallow names the house. You know which star in your Seven Stars has gone sour. Now you can call it home.

choices.text: Hear it out: your Field Fire has been set loose on a rival family's millet terraces

effects.log: The swallow names the slope. You know the star. Now you can call it home.

choices.text: Hear it out: the ferry Lantern is being hung on the wrong bank, to wreck boats for their cargo

effects.log: The swallow names the river. You know the star. Now you can call it home.

choices.text: Shut your ears. Your keepers would not

effects.log: You tell the swallow it is mistaken. It is not mistaken. A turned fire burns three years for every one, and it will not wait while you decide what to believe.

events.text: A swallow from the coast and the kiln country lands on your ridge out of turn, in high summer, which swallows do not do. It has carried its news a long way: a keeper of yours there has turned.

choices.text: Hear it out: your Kiln is firing day and night for a rebel lord's forge

effects.log: The swallow names the hillside. You know the star. Now you can call it home.

choices.text: Hear it out: your Beacon is being lit falsely for a bribe

effects.log: The swallow names the hill. You know the star. Now you can call it home.

effects.log: The swallow names the lineage hall. You know the star. Now you can call it home.

events.text: A swallow that nests under the eaves of a county office comes to you with ink on its tail feathers and a story about the clerk who keeps your lamp.

choices.text: Hear it out: the Lamp of the Court is reading forged deeds as true

effects.log: The swallow names the office. You know the star. Now you can call it home.

choices.text: Shut your ears. Your keepers would not

effects.log: You tell the swallow it is mistaken. It is not mistaken. A turned fire burns three years for every one, and it will not wait while you decide what to believe.

events.text: You go and look at a keeper the swallows named: a person who once took your fire with both hands and promised. The fire in their keeping burns hard and greedy now. They see you on the roof and do not look away.

choices.text: Speak to them from the ridge, once, before anything else

ok.log: You talk until dark about what the fire was for. Somewhere in it the keeper starts to cry, and in the morning the fire is a kitchen fire again, and the star in you cools to red. It is very rare. It happens.

fail.log: "It is mine now," they say. "You gave it." You did. That is the trouble with giving. You fly off with the words stuck in your throat.

choices.text: Leave it a year longer, and hope

effects.log: You leave it. Hope is a kind of fuel too, and it burns fast. Call a Fire Home, if you mean to, before it runs.

choices.text: Flare on their roof so the whole village sees what they did

effects.log: Their roof ridge smokes and the whole village comes out to look, and looks at them, and knows. Shame is a kind of fire too. It does not put the turned one out. (Ash +1)
